The pole is a retrospective 'spell it out' detector: it fires on a token that is a piece of a long multi-piece word - a rare, technical, proper-noun, foreign or identifier-like word that the tokenizer splits into several BPE pieces - peaking on an interior piece (Chem|oin|vest|ig|ative -> 'vest' 1.9, Ch|aler|mb|ure -> 'aler' 1.7, Sub|m|arg|inal -> 'arg' 1.5, a|theros|cl|er|otic -> 'er' 1.3, un|inform|ative -> 'inform' 1.0, Es|cher|ich|ia -> 'cher' 0.65, cerc|op|it|hec|ida|e -> 'it' 0.5, Amazon K|inesis -> 'inesis' 0.6) and it also fires on interior tokens of multi-digit numerals ('range(10)' -> '0' 0.28, '13' -> '3' 0.21, '1,204,000' -> '4' 0.24); in a matched frame that piece beats an ordinary whole word in the same slot by a wide margin (anthraquinones 0.43 vs chemicals 0.14, chrysanthemum 0.30 vs flower 0.08, cercopithecidae 0.51 vs monkey 0.07, piezophily 0.33 vs stress 0.10). Plain prose made of common single-piece words stays near its 0.03-0.15 baseline - even long single-token words are inert ('downloadable' 0.08) - with a context-dependent tail to about 0.3 on ordinary words, and it is not a next-token predictor (Jacobian-lens kurtosis 3.7, lens agreement 0%, incoherent promoted set).

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a conventionalized local unit strongly cued by the immediately preceding 1-2 tokens: either the continuation of a split multi-token word (ochondria, -ynthesis, violin-ist) or the cued second half of a fixed collocation (at->least, greater->than, According to->the, Neil->Armstrong, stepped->out). The same surface token without its licensing left context (least after was, the after Listen to, Armstrong after young) drives little activity.

This pole fires when the current token is the constrained completion of the preceding one or two tokens: the second half of a fixed phrase or collocation ('fell silent', 'through Sunday', 'on average', 'at sea level', 'According to the'), a compound or split subword ('protons', 'Seine', 'Photosynthesis'), or the obligatory filler of a slot opened by the previous head ('def' name, 'WHERE' condition, 'one' quantifier, list copula). The identical token in an open context where many continuations are possible ('Her silent', 'alien egg', 'They add', 'bought the') fires weakly or not at all, and distant words outside the local frame do not gate it.

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a stereotyped 1-2-token chunk: modal after a subject pronoun (I/They+can 0.37-0.43, I+will 0.26, but You/We+can 0.0), particle after a posture or stative verb (sat/stood/lay/sits+on 0.14-0.28, stepped+out 0.23), a conventionalized noun collocation (at+noon, interest+rates, the+onions, cold+wind, main+loop, was+born in a relative clause), an interrogative Where at clause onset (quoted Where itself 0.22, bare Where via following is 0.26), a stem+subword or number+digit completion (Photosynthesis, light-years, re-election, Apollo 11, 3.9, a.m.), or a list/argument comma. It stays near zero on the same surface tokens outside those chunks (noun can 0.07, near-noon 0.05, sentence-initial Noon 0.0, turned+on 0.0, recalled+on 0.10, relative where itself 0.07, discourse commas ~0.0), at sentence-initial position 0 (scan mean exactly 0.0), and on unpredictable content words, which context modulation explains better than token identity despite its 0.76 R2.

This pole fires on the head (second) word of a two-word noun compound: a common noun used attributively immediately followed by the noun it classifies or supplies the argument for ('price tag', 'culture clash', 'system partition', 'information sharing', 'bank failures', 'house visits'). The same head word goes near-silent when it follows a determiner, numeral, adjective or participle ('the tag', 'big tag', 'quick partition', 'swimming pool') or when it comes first ('tag price'), the modifier noun itself never fires, and strength is largest for abstract/event/relational heads (clash, swap, change, war, decision, failure, visit, gap) and weak for concrete object compounds (coffee cup, car door).

This pole fires when the current token completes a locally highly predictable continuation of the immediately preceding 1-2 tokens (a frequent bigram or fixed collocation such as the+sunrise, second+half, pleaded+not, stared+at), across topics and token identities; keeping the same peak token but swapping the preceding word for an incongruous one sharply reduces activation.

The pole fires retrospectively on the token that continues a lexical or identifier unit begun in the immediately preceding token(s): a subword piece inside one word (up/cycled, snow/ed, parahipp/ocampal, Jer/sey), the tail of a CamelCase, dotted-path or code identifier (XML/StreamReader, openapi/.roots), or the predictable tail of a fixed multiword term, sequence or label slot (data/matrix, track/back, Cartesian/MR, q/rs, ISBN/:). The same surface token fires weakly or not at all as a fresh word onset or after an unrelated cue (stored matrix, crackback, data table), and words after the peak leave firing unchanged.

This pole fires retrospectively on the head word immediately following an approximative or precision-degree modifier (almost, nearly, virtually, essentially, partly, pretty much, exactly), or on the stem completing a semi-/half- prefixed compound (semi-flexible, semi-arid, half-life); deleting or replacing the modifier while keeping the head word abolishes the peak.

Fires on the word 'official' used as an adjective or adverb meaning formally sanctioned or authorised status ('official trailer/website/figures/capacity', 'officially announced', 'now official'), and on its cognates in other languages (French officiel(lement), German offiziell, Spanish oficial(mente)), peaking on the token that completes the 'offic-' stem (e.g. 'iel', 'izi', 'ical'), at about 0.55-0.9 of max. It is much weaker (about 0.15-0.35 of max) for the noun sense 'a government official' / 'officials' and for near-synonyms 'unofficial', 'formally', 'formal', 'authorized'. It is essentially silent on 'office', 'officer', other status adjectives ('state', 'verified', 'personal', 'final'), and on the very first token of a text.

The positive pole is a right-edge detector for a lexicalized multi-token designation: it peaks on the token that completes a fixed term, abbreviation, proper name or idiom rather than on any word - ' service' closing 'quality of service' (2.5-5.9), ' life' closing 'quality of life' (3.2) and 'end of life' (4.0), ' birth' closing 'date of birth' (5.8) and 'place of birth' (0.9-2.1), ' death' closing 'cause of death' (1.4), ' Service' closing 'terms of service' (3.0), ' sale' closing 'point of sale' (4.5), ' day' closing 'time of day' (4.8), 'F' closing DOF (3.4-4.9), 'B' closing DOB (2.8), 'V' closing POV (4.1), 'A' closing COA (3.1), ' Boh' closing 'Niels Bohr' (1.9), ' in' closing 'join in' (2.3), ' down' closing 'stopping down' (2.3), and the 'of' that closes a fixed prepositional frame such as 'at the time of' (2.7) or 'in event of' (3.1); the word alone is neither necessary nor sufficient, because the scan's other 17 occurrences of ' service' read 0.00-0.47, ' birth' reads 0.00 in 'assigned at birth', ' death' 0.00-0.67 in 'rate/perinatal/sudden/cell death', ' view' 0.00-0.16 outside 'point of view', and every ' day' in the scan is at most 0.11 ('the end of the day', 'the next day'), while breaking the unit collapses the peak. Breaking the designation kills it on the same words: inserting a determiner ('quality of the service' 0.09 vs 2.50, 'terms of the service' 0.11 vs 2.99, 'cause of the death' 0.22 vs 0.98, 'quality of the life' 0.66 vs 3.18), reordering the compound ('service quality' 0.10 vs 2.50), spelling out an abbreviation ('depth of field' 0.21 vs DOF 3.39, 'Enter date here' 0.11 vs 'Enter DOB here' 2.83), or swapping the name ('Niels Borh' 0.23 vs 1.87, 'Tour de Suisse' 0.09 vs 'Tour de France' 0.40, 'DOG'/'POT'/'COX' 0.07-0.26 vs DOF/POV/COA) - while an unrelated substitution ('hospitals' for 'clinics') leaves it at 2.50 vs 2.50; leftovers outside the claim: membership of the unit list is lexical rather than semantic ('quality of care' 0.28, 'bill of materials' 0.10, 'standard of living' 0.14 stay at the floor although near-synonyms fire), and the mechanism is retrospective (zero-ablating the pole moves next-token KL by at most 1e-2 with no coherent promoted token set; Jacobian kurtosis 3.6, lens agreement 0), with the negative pole peaking on fragments of unfamiliar strings (' hp' in 'Jodhpur', ' imers' in 'heterodimers', ' led' in Norwegian 'ledes'), the un-assembled complement of this right-edge feature.

The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the head word of a hedged scalar relation - the preposition, particle, comparative or small-amount noun that states how far something sits from a reference point - and it fires strongly only when that word is immediately preceded by a small-degree downtoner: 'just under/over/past/before/after/outside/inside/beyond/above/below/behind/ahead/up/off/short of/shy of/left of/right of/south of', 'a little more/less/lower', 'slightly off/below', 'a bit behind', 'shortly before', 'a small/slight/tiny chance', 'a little bit/something' (measured peaks 4.5-14.3, e.g. 'just under' 13.6 and 'a little more' 6.5 against 'under' 1.2 and 'more' 0.0 with no left modifier). The same relational head after an intensifier instead of a downtoner ('very', 'well', 'much', 'a lot', 'far'), after a non-small approximator ('about', 'almost', 'nearly', 'roughly', 'exactly'), with no left modifier, or after the same downtoner in front of an ordinary noun ('a little dog/cake/water') stays at 0.0-3.1, and 'just' plus a non-relational word ('just the/a/want/like/because/thinking') is inert, while a preceding measure phrase ('nine miles east of', 'three hours after', 'two feet under') gives the same head-word peak at a weaker 1.5-3.8 and colon clock times ('3:05', '1:31', '2:03') are a further weaker offshoot (2.5-6.3 on the last digit, with plain numbers like '199'/'305'/'1990' silent).

Peaks retrospectively on the second element of a locally highly predictable two-token unit — negation after a modal (would not), a time preposition after a weekday (Friday at), a magnitude or unit word after a number (12 percent, 13 billion), an ordinal/determiner completing a noun phrase (the second, watched the), or the second subword of a familiar word or tag (Tok-yo, Ham-let, Se-ine, body) — when the preceding 1-2 tokens strongly constrain it; the same surface token in an unpredictable bigram, or a rare subword continuation, is predicted inactive.

L3/N4398- is a stored-token-string (n-gram) detector rather than a token detector: it fires at the current token when the token immediately before it - sometimes the two before - matches the first half of a memorised two- or three-token string, i.e. the joint inside a rare word ('out' in Maci Book|out 2.74, 'ot' in Disc|otek 1.68, 'ond' in Rosam|ond 1.16, 'im' in poly|imide 1.51, 'ort' in Skv|ort|zov 1.34, 'C' in CAM|C 1.65, '8' in sha3|84 0.77) or the second word of a stored collocation, proper name, product name or technical term (' Out' in The Great| Outdoors 5.04, ' Public' in GNU General| Public 2.10, ' Natural' in Department of| Natural 1.39, ' league' in major| league 1.51, ' account' after social 1.23, ' acid' after metabolic 1.05, ' tape' after police 0.94, ' Pictures' after Universal 0.76). The string, not the token id, carries the feature: the same token is at baseline under any other predecessor (' Public' 1.78 after 'General' vs 0.02 after 'the'; ' league' 1.51 after 'major' vs <0.19 after 'youth'; ' Out' 5.04 after 'Great' vs 1.18 after 'Big'), other continuations of the same prefix do not fire (GNU General| Assembly 0.02, Department of| History 0.00, Universal| Studios 0.01, police| car 0.06), strength is graded by how much of the stored prefix is present (GNU General| Public 2.10 > General| Public 1.78 > the| Public 0.02; Department of| Natural 1.39 > Office of| Natural 0.93 > Bureau of| Natural <0.30), and the mechanism is retrospective: strength is fixed by the left context alone (2.102 with either 'License' or 'Licence' after the trigger; 0.792 for ' de' with either 'Ville' or 'Crillon' after it; the unspaced retokenisation 'Great'+'Outdoors' still fires at 4.88), the Jacobian lens is flat (kurtosis 3.3, 0% overlap with the logit lens) and zero-ablating the pole leaves the strongest continuations (' Public' after GNU General, ' Natural' after Department of) unchanged.

The negative pole tracks stative, non-agentive predication: it peaks on base-form copula and stative predicates (' be', ' have', ' need', ' depend', ' require', ' resemble', ' equal', ' mean', ' include', ' involve', ' seem', ' appear', ' weigh') and on relational nominalisations such as 'variability', 'prevalence', 'incidence', 'similarity', 'correlation' together with the preposition that introduces their complement (' of', ' between', ' with', ' for'). It falls to near zero when the same slot holds an agentive/eventive verb ('build', 'destroy', 'attack', 'give', 'make'), when the clause subject is an agentive human ('They', 'She', 'The authors') rather than impersonal 'It'/'This', and on concrete nouns in the identical frame ('the box of the table' = 0.03 vs 'the variability of the system' = 1.10).

This pole reads the word, not the token: it fires when the word being read names a specific structure of the body's skeleton and limbs - named bones and bone adjectives (femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, ulna, patella, carpal, calcaneus, iliac, femoral, tibial), joints and limb regions (hip, knee, elbow, wrist, groin, armpit, thigh, calf, shoulder), skeletal muscles (gastrocnemius, gluteus, sartorius, deltoid) and some English bone compounds (thighbone, shinbone) - peaking 5-13 on the Latin bone names and 1-5 on the rest, with other named organic structures (aorta, pharynx, trachea, rectum, anus, ileum) at 1-3; the peak lands on the word's last fragment, and the identical token 'ula' fires at 8.0 inside 'fibula' but 0.3 inside 'uvula' and 0.1 inside 'nebula'. It stays near its ~0.1 baseline on internal organs and organ adjectives (liver, heart, kidney, cardiac, renal, hepatic, gastric, pulmonary), on generic tissue words (bone, joint, muscle, tendon, cartilage, vertebra), on skin/face parts (skin, eye, tooth, lip), on disease words (arthritis, aneurysm, carcinoma) and on non-body words that share the same final token (humorous, cardiac, special, cubicle), and it is several-fold weaker when the same structure is named in plain English (femur 7.4 vs 'thigh bone' 2.0, patella 4.5 vs 'kneecap' 0.3, iliac 12.9 vs 'hip' 1.5).

This pole is a retrospective phrase-medial extension signal: it fires on tokens that continue an open constituent (clause verbs, VP-extending prepositions, modals, clause-linking medial pronouns, medial determiners, descriptive adjectives/adverbs), with strength building over the first few tokens of a clause; it stays near zero on constituent onsets (sentence-initial tokens, e.g. 'The' is silent across 16 occurrences) and on tokens that close a predictable unit (complement nouns like 'school/cake/mat', complement verbs after modals or 'to'). The Jacobian lens shows no coherent upcoming-token set (kurtosis ~3.5, zero lens overlap), so it reacts to read context rather than preparing specific next tokens.

N1360+ is a retrospective 'name-completion' detector: it fires on the token at which a specific, familiar name for a concrete thing becomes complete - the whole token when the name is a single token ('calcium', 'rabbits', 'Sudan', 'Austria', 'diabetes') and the word-final subword piece when the name is spelled across tokens ('occus' in Streptococcus, 'ella' in Salmonella, 'oodle' in Poodle, 'cloth' in dishcloth) - including the digit that completes a written year ('0' in 'the late 1800s'). It is strongest (0.8-1.4 on the pole's 2.11 scale) when two to four such names of things in the world - substances and foods, organisms, diseases and pathogens, products - are enumerated in one expository sentence, and it falls below 0.5 when those names are replaced by generic category words or abstractions ('light, exercise or sleep', 'a first organism, a second organism') or when the word is one the model has no whole-word entry for (pangolin, okapi, bassoon, and quartz/feldspar in a plain list of minerals).

The pole fires on a token that names a marked degree of something's worth, adequacy or capability - the deficiency/incapacity family (inferior, worthless and worthlessness, helpless(ness), powerless, hopeless(ness), incompetent and incompetence, incapable, inadequate, ineffective, insignificant, negligible, imperfect and imperfection, futile, failure, weakness(es), defective, disposable, blame/blaming) and the eminence family (perfection, superior and superiority, excellence, greatness, mastery, dignity, precious, worth, worthy, unworthy, merit) - and is graded by what is being graded: strongest when the word grades a person or a person's act ('He felt worthless' 1.65x the scan max, 'He was worthless' 0.93x) and weaker, though still above the active threshold, when it grades an object or is used in a non-evaluative sense ('the inferior vena cava' 0.58x, 'Superior Court' 0.36x, 'This product is inferior' 0.79x); the same words in other languages (inférieur, supérieur, inferiore, wertlos) stay near zero, as do their abstract nominal forms only when the stem is not a worth stem (darkness, sadness, kindness, fairness, rudeness). It stays at the floor (under 0.05x max) for everyday quality adjectives and for other dimensions - good, great, excellent, superb, outstanding, bad, poor, nice, fine; magnitude: important, significant, substantial, crucial, essential, major; raw potency: strong, powerful, weak, dominant; money: price, cost, rich, wealthy, expensive; social rank and honour: rank, status, prestige, respect, honour, fame, shame; emotion: angry, sad, happy, afraid; aesthetics: beautiful, ugly - so it is not an evaluation, valence, frequency or abstract-noun-suffix detector.

The negative pole fires on the tokens that state a specific amount of a measurable property - a numeral or number word together with the unit or measured noun it quantifies (2 kilometres, 300 kilograms, 40 metres deep, 8 hours, 12 tonnes, 20 degrees, 500 litres, forty-five minutes) - peaking on or just after the numeral and its unit noun and staying up across the rest of the measure phrase. Activation drops sharply, typically to under half, when the same property is described qualitatively or evaluated with no amount (very heavy, quite warm, a long way, deep and cold, exhausting, a lot, many), while swapping one amount for another (20 degrees vs 30 degrees, 10 vs 12 kilometres) leaves it essentially unchanged.

This pole retrospectively fires on the vocabulary of software packaging and developer tooling: the names package managers and package manifests give to artifacts (cask, brew/Homebrew, formula, tap, gem, Gemfile, bundle, podspec, node_modules, EXTERNAL_DIR, .jar/.ttf/.gradle, javax.ws.rs.ext, the RubyGems constraint ~>) and the names of libraries that sit in a dependency list (Boost, FreeType, autorest, Jekyll, rubocop, scikit-learn), firing hardest where several of those terms cluster in a manifest line or an install/upgrade command. It stays at the scan floor on ordinary prose that uses the same surface words in their everyday sense (a wooden cask, a gem sparkling, brewed tea, the quadratic formula, the hub of a wheel) and on general software prose that names no package (the compiler, the repository, the API, Kubernetes), all of which measure 0.04-0.25 against a maximum of 7.14.

Fires on a sub-word token that ends exactly at a Greek/Latin combining-form prefix, linking vowel included, when the token is a bare prefix waiting for its stem or used on its own: 'micro'/' micro'/' Micro' strongest (~0.8-1.0 of max, e.g. ' micro|flora', 'micro|seconds', 'a new micro'), then 'tetra' ('tet|ra'), 'angio' ('ang|io'), 'icosa' ('icos|ah'), 'andro' ('And|ro'), 'xylo' ('xy|lo'), 'polyc', ' macro' (~0.5-0.9), and weaker for ' nano', ' mega', ' mono', ' poly', ' multi', ' mill', ' hex', ' hydro' (~0.25-0.5). It stays near zero on whole-word tokens that only contain such a prefix (' microwave', ' microscopic', ' microtime', ' nanoparticles', ' psychology'), on fragments cut before the linking vowel (' angi', ' cy', ' tri', ' di'), on ordinary words, and at the first token of a sequence. The context before the token barely matters.

Detects the letter c/C when it names the C programming language family, retrospectively. The strongest case (8-18) is the lowercase 'c' inside a copyright mark '(c)' right after 'Copyright'/'COPYRIGHT'/'Licensed', as in source-file license headers; uppercase '(C)' is much weaker (2-4) and '(x)', '(b)', a bare '©' or '(c)' with no Copyright word stay near 0. Moderate activity (3-8) comes when ' C' names the language (in C, ANSI C, C++, C#, C/C++, Objective-C, the C:\ drive) or on the token that disambiguates an earlier ' C' as the language (' language'/' programming' after ' C'), and on C-ecosystem tokens ('.h' in #include <...h>, malloc, free, printf). The letter C used non-programmatically (vitamin C, grade C) and other language names (Python, Java, R, D, F#, CUDA) stay near 0.

Fires on a prefix (unary) operator token that opens an operand where the syntax expects an operand, not an operator, in code or arithmetic: above all a space-preceded unary minus ' -' right after a binary/comparison/logical operator, '=', ':=', ',', 'return' or a keyword ('5 - -3', '3 + -5', '&& -y', 'i == -1', 'foo(a, -1)', 'return -1'), strongest (~3-5.7) when the preceding token is itself an operator. Other operand-opening prefixes are weaker (unary ' +' ~2.5, ' ~'/' !' ~1-1.5, a regex-literal '/', an ObjC message ' [' in code), while the same ' -' used as a binary operator after an operand ('x - 1', '5 - 3', '3 - 2' in prose) and literals without a sign stay near zero.

Retrospective, and the weak side of a two-lobed neuron: the sharp negative pole is a firearms/hunting detector ('hunting' 7.8, 'cartridge' 8.0, 'rifle' 5.9), while the positive pole fires on tokens that carry technical notation or technical naming rather than narrative content - LaTeX math delimiters and closers ('$$', '}}', '}' followed by '\', ';' glued to a closing '$'), markup and identifier syntax ('@android:', '<name', '_name', '("'), and the second element of technical compound terms ('orthogonal', 'beam splitter'). Plain narrative prose, and any firearms/hunting text, stays at the floor (peak below 0.35 of max).

N2435- is a retrospective span-end detector: it fires on the token that closes a marked span opened earlier in the same line or block - the '>' of a '<...>' type-argument/generic list ('List<Package>', 'std::vector<std::string>'), the closing '*' or '_' of markdown emphasis, the '"]' that ends a quoted JSON/PHP array, the closing '\Vert'/'$' of LaTeX math, a closing tag or ')' in code, and the field terminators '####' at a heading line start, a run of spaces after '#if', and the '=' after a multi-item assignment target. It tracks span closure, not the characters themselves: the same '>' used as a spaced comparison operator ('a > b', '5 > 3'), commas in simple prose lists, and ordinary content words stay near zero, while prose appositive commas ('include, for example', 'The report, which was long') and the idiom 'much of a' are acknowledged residuals that also fire.

This pole fires retrospectively on the current token when it is the highly predictable completion of the immediately preceding one to three tokens: the second half of a fixed collocation or compound (sea level), a range endpoint (Tuesday through Sunday), or an operator-plus-argument frame (return a + b, at noon, images of), with strength scaling with how constraining the local frame is, while the identical token in a non-constraining context evokes little or no response. It also carries a weak position-zero baseline (about 5% of its max) on whatever token begins a sequence.

Strong firing occurs retrospectively on a content word that completes an explicit specification frame set up 1-5 tokens earlier (a number/ordinal before a noun such as eight-characters or second-half, a time number before p, WHERE before a column, because-of before a cause noun). The Jacobian and logit lenses are flat and incoherent (kurtosis 3.4, 0% agreement), showing no upcoming-token preparation, and weak ~0.2 firing on frequent tokens like 'the' is baseline noise.

Fires, retrospectively, on the token that conventionally completes the phrase underway: the expected collocation, named entity, scheduling or legal-boilerplate term, code or math syntax, or subword completion. Amplitude is graded by constraint: content keywords in matching formal/news gist respond most strongly (fraud, stock, year, via the g+u+ regime), function-word and subword completions more weakly (at, in, ine, world, via the g-u- double-negative regime). The same token outside its conventional context, or an incongruent substitute in the same slot, drives it to baseline or below, which a bare trigger-token list cannot predict.

This pole fires retrospectively on two triggers: (a) digit tokens inside a four-digit number read as a calendar year, peaking on an early digit (e.g. the '9' in 'In 1969', the '8' in 'the year 1847'), strongest for plausible Western years and silent on identical digits in counts ('count 1847/1969'), quantities ('11 cats', '500 mg', '13 billion') or implausible years ('7351', '4823'); (b) the word-form ' museum' in any context ('The museum', 'toured the museum'), staying silent on near-synonym building nouns (library, gallery, monument, artifact, prison).

Fires retrospectively on a noun or verb token that reports or assigns a position on an ordered evaluative or measurement scale — school, medical, product-condition, sports, or slope grades, ranks, scores, indices, acuity levels, or equivalents — with peak strength on explicit grade/rank tokens used in a classification or measurement frame.

This pole fires on the second token of a locally predictable, high-frequency two-token continuation: a determiner, preposition, conjunction, or noun that completes the phrase opened by the immediately preceding token (verb or preposition plus determiner, adjective plus noun in an entrenched collocation such as 'negative charge' or 'not guilty', noun plus 'and' joining clauses, ORDER plus BY). Activation is jointly driven by the peak token and its licensor, so keeping the peak token but replacing the preceding word with one that breaks the collocation collapses activity, while changes outside the local pair leave it intact.

This neuron pole retrospectively detects lexical items denoting finiteness, discreteness, countability, or boundedness (such as 'finite', 'finiteness', 'discrete', 'countable', 'bounded', and 'limited') across mathematical, statistical, and general contexts. It activates maximally on explicit statements of finite cardinality or discreteness, shows moderate activation on antonymous bounds ('infinite', 'uncountable', 'unbounded'), and remains inactive on continuous, dense, smooth, or unbounded non-discrete concepts.

Retrospective detector for an approximate (vague, small) amount phrase: the pole peaks on the vague-quantity head of "a little X", "a few X", "a bit of X" or "a couple of X" -- most strongly on ' little' and on the ' of' that follows ' bit' or ' couple' -- and it tracks the construction rather than the word, since ' little' stays quiet as a size adjective ("the little girl", 0.37), in the negative-polarity idiom ("Little did he know", 0.00) and as a bare quantifier ("little hope", 0.12; "Few people", 0.09). Exact and large quantity words do not fire it ("a lot of" 0.14-0.49, "a piece of" 0.48, "a number of" 0.04, "a dozen" 0.23, "several" 0.00, "many" 0.13, "plenty of" 0.10) and neither do exact numerals ("45 minutes" 0.12, "in 2017" 0.17); every strong (>0.5) activation is in the SwiGLU g+u- regime (the diffuse <=0.5 g-u+ response to ordinary content words is a separate broadcast regime), and these leftovers are outside the claim: determiners and quantifiers right after light verbs ("could use a" 2.85, "learns a" 2.71, "take some time" 1.99, "snap a few" 1.83), the word-piece 'm' in identifiers ("dbmigrate", 4.35), measure nouns such as ' seconds' ("a few seconds" 3.10, which fire even after 'several' and are themselves top token-identity drivers), and numerals in approximative frames ("an hour or two" 2.34, "or three" 2.25).

The positive pole fires on the token that completes a gendered civilian title of address (Mr, Ms, Mrs, Miss, Mister, Madam, Mme, Monsieur; more weakly Madame, Herr, Señor), peaking on the abbreviation period of 'Mr.'/'Ms.'/'Mrs.' (~9-12) or on the title token itself when no period follows (~7-9), whether or not a personal name follows ('Mr. Coffee', 'Mr. Universe', 'Thank you, Mr. President'). Professional or noble titles (Dr ~2.5, Prof ~1, Sir ~1), other abbreviation periods ('p.m.', 'U.S.', 'St.') and bare names stay near zero; its Jacobian-lens output promotes the same title tokens (' Mr', '先生'), so it is a retrospective 'Mister/Missus title just read' detector rather than a predictor of the upcoming surname.

The negative pole fires on a closed family of formal, Latin-derived process and planning words - 'consider / consideration / considering', 'research', 'study', 'explore', 'improve', 'seek', 'mitigate', 'feasible', 'sufficient', 'assessment', 'analysis', ' per capita', 'red tourism', and the fixed phrases 'Did you know' and 'not only ... but also' - and on the function words (' of', ' that') that continue those phrases, but only when the word sits in the hedged, deliberative frame of written expository prose: after a deontic or necessity marker (should, ought to, must, need to, have to, 'recommend that you', 'it is important to'), after 'worth', after source-introducing 'According to', or inside those fixed constructions. It stays silent on the same words as the plain finite predicate of a simple declarative ('we consider the options', 'I know the answer', 'we study / we explore the proposal'), when 'will' replaces a deontic modal, when a near-synonym outside the family is used ('should examine / assess / evaluate / review'), and in casual narrative text; its opposite pole instead fires on policy-action and goal vocabulary (phase out, eradicate, fight against, campaign, priority), and every top negative peak is in the same g+u- SwiGLU regime, so this is one job, not two.

Fires on the word naming a hostile blow, attack or (more weakly) intense attention that the sentence subject RECEIVES, read inside a patient-side frame such as 'come/be under X', 'take/taking (a lot of) X', 'get/got (a lot of) X', 'got X-ed by', 'draw/face X' (e.g. 'under fire', 'taking heat', 'took a beating/hit/knock', 'got hammered/beaten by', 'came under attack/criticism', 'got a lot of hate/love/praise'); strongest for violence/heat metaphors (beating, heat, fire, hammered, hit), weaker for criticism/attack/praise, near zero for neutral received objects (break, loss, money, review, scrutiny, funding, views). The same words used outside the receiving frame (literal 'turn up the heat', 'on fire', 'opened fire', 'beat the eggs/record') stay inactive, so the pole tracks 'subject is on the receiving end of a hit/attack', not token identity.

This pole is a retrospective detector of local contextual fit: it fires when the current token is a fluent, unsurprising continuation of the preceding ~1-4 tokens (a familiar collocation, a grammatical function word in place, the inside of a word or year), and it goes quiet when the peak token is surprising given its immediate prefix, such as a semantic mismatch, an ungrammatical pairing, or a broken construction. The same surface token (e.g. ' wind', ' of', ' a') is active after a fitting prefix and inactive after an unfitting one, and words after the peak do not matter.

Retrospective: the pole fires on the token that continues or completes a multi-token licensing frame set up by earlier tokens in the same sentence -- e.g. the complement verb after 'ruled that the <noun>', the 'to' closing a 'from'-range, the second verb after '<action> and', a pronoun continuing a greeting opener, or the consequent noun after 'then the' -- with activation driven by those earlier frame tokens (mean attribution distance ~1.6; single-token swaps of the frame opener collapse it). The same surface token in a bare frame with no licensing context (e.g. 'was' in 'The contract was void.', 'stared' in 'She stared at the wall.', 'at' in 'They arrived at noon.') stays near silent, so the pole tracks frame completion, not token identity.

L4/N4851- fires retrospectively on the reference-frame word: the token that says a noun or a place is to be read against something else, peaking on the modifier ' relative' in any sense (1.7-4.6: 'the relative cost', 'relative to X', 'my relative'), then on ' comparative' (1.8-3.4), ' respective' (1.6), ' characteristic' (1.5), ' absolute' (1.3), the locative root ' loc' in location/located/loci (1.3-1.7) and ' sobre' (0.9), with the adverbs 'relatively'/'respectively'/'comparatively' only around the active line (0.65-1.25). It also fires on the genitive ' of' only when the noun before it names a place or a position ('the location/region/zone/place/position/edge/site of X', 0.7-1.8) and not after ordinary nouns ('the price/size/weight/number/purpose/surface of X', <=0.45), and stays at baseline on resemblance words that name no frame ('similar', 'equivalent', 'comparable', 'related', 'relation', 'relevant', 'respect', 'comparison'), on other academic adjectives ('significant', 'structural', 'theoretical'), on the bare stems 'relatives' and 'relativity', and on any trigger sitting at a text's first position (no leading space).

The negative pole fires on a relative pronoun at the moment it opens a relative clause: a definite D-word or wh-pronoun (German der/die/das/den/dem/denen, Danish-Norwegian der/den/det/de/dem, Dutch die, English which/whose/whom, Spanish (el/lo) cual, French dont/qui) sitting in the clause-linking slot immediately after a comma or a preposition, where it refers back to an antecedent (peak 2.3-5.7 there). The same form as a determiner after a verb or at a sentence start, or as an interrogative, demonstrative, indefinite article or non-D-word marker, stays near zero: 'Ich sehe den Mann' 0.0 and 'Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch' 0.0 on the D-word, 'de partij' 0.07, 'Die Frau steht dort' 0.04, 'Which book did you read last year?' peaks 0.20, '¿Cuál es tu respuesta?' 0.70, 'Qui a fait cela?' 0.26, 'dieser' 0.37 even after a comma, English 'that' 0.0 after a comma, 'dass/weil/because' 0.05-0.32; because the decision is made at the pronoun itself, a comma followed by an article in a German list ('Der Hund, die Katze...' 3.48) is a predicted false positive, as the disambiguating noun has not been read yet.

The pole fires on the punctuation that closes a written unit: the sentence-final full stop, exclamation mark or question mark, and above all the fused forms that also break the line ('.' < '.
' < '.

'), which is why the same closure is amplified several-fold at the edge of an enclosed block - a period inside a /* ... */ comment line measures 2.0-2.9 against 0.28 in plain prose, the line-leading ' *' and '@' of a doc comment 0.8-3.5, and the word or two that open a quotation right after a double quote 0.6-3.2 ('"The bus', '"I am'), though not for every opener ('"The plan' stays at 0.00). It is not about topic, and not about quotation as such: plain unquoted prose peaks on its sentence-final stop (ten of ten such sentences measured 0.23-0.30, clear of the 0.174 active threshold), while the first token of any text (0.004-0.012), the content words inside an unclosed clause, and a sentence whose closing stop is deleted stay near zero, so a stop-less version of a sentence reaches only about half the peak of the same sentence with its stop.

Pole N1073+ fires when a clause is anchored to an earlier time than the narrative present, and it peaks on the token that completes the framer rather than on any fixed word: the ' in' of 'back in …', the ' then'/' when' of 'back then'/'back when …', the ' of' in 'in the days of X' and 'in those/old/earlier days', the child/teen noun or its closing comma in 'when I was a little girl/teenager,' and 'when you were a kid,', the ' to' of 'used to …'/'prior to …', the ' before' of 'long before …'/'the days before …', and the ' time' of 'at the time (of)'/'at that time' (all 1.6–6.4 on the pole's 6.4 scale). Present- and future-referring counterparts of these framers fall below 0.5 ('at the moment', 'these days', 'in the coming days', 'long after us', 'is used to', '… will … in 2089'), as do non-temporal uses of the same words ('in the drawer', 'give it back', 'prior notice') and ordinary past-tense narration with no time frame ('She bought milk'); the exceptions and weak parts are that the 'when I was …' clause still gives ~2 when only its tense is made present, that numerals in past date expressions ('from 1933 to 1935', 'in 1970') give only an inconstant 0.4–2 in isolation (higher only inside an already date-rich passage), and that the 'at the/a time (of/when)' formula also fires for future or present events; the output direction promotes period/history vocabulary ('era', 'history', '年代', '岁月', 'historians'), so the pole marks a passage as set in an earlier period rather than preparing one particular next token.

The negative pole encodes the information-security countermeasure concept: it is active (0.6+ on its 2.57-point scale) on encryption vocabulary ('encrypt', 'encrypted', 'encryption', disk or backup encryption), on authentication in its technical compounds ('Message Authentication', 'two-factor/biometric authentication', 'cryptographic authentication'), and on the other mechanisms and operations of computer security - verification and signatures, public-key cryptography, TPM/HSM security modules, intrusion detection, antivirus, and control verbs such as verify, unlock, protect, ensure, enforce, block and alert - including generic words like 'technology', 'algorithm' or 'system' when they sit inside a passage that is explaining such a mechanism. It stays near zero when the same strings are used outside computing security (authentication of a painting, Homeland Security, pension or physical security), in ordinary software prose, and on the attack side (hacker, malware, phishing, injection, breach), which instead drives this neuron's positive pole and is exactly the vocabulary the negative pole suppresses under the Jacobian lens; the concept must be corroborated by context, so 'Encryption is covered in chapter four' remains near zero while one preceding security sentence lifts 'encrypt' from 0.6 to 2.7.

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes a frequent, overlearned local continuation: the familiar second half of an idiomatic collocation ('at least', 'can't', 'pinch of salt'), a canonical syntactic bigram (preposition plus 'the', 'was' plus past participle, 'for i' plus 'in', 'def' plus a common name), or a frequent subword split ('Photosynthesis', "m'appelle"). The same word after an unfamiliar partner, or an unfamiliar word in the same constraining slot, stays low.

The pole is a term detector for search-engine marketing: it fires on the vocabulary webmasters and search advertisers use about a page's standing in web search - 'SEO', 'Yoast', 'search engine(s)', 'keywords', 'Pay Per Click'/'PPC', 'rank'/'ranking', 'optimise'/'optimisation'/'optimised', 'backlinks', 'SERP', 'sitemap', 'noindex', 'Googlebot', 'meta description', 'domain authority', 'Search Console', 'webmaster tools', and 'Google'/'Yahoo' named as search engines (also the equivalents in other languages, e.g. 排名/优化, 搜索引擎, posicionamiento en buscadores) - plus, more weakly, the page-head markup that carries search metadata ('meta description', 'meta robots'/'noindex', 'link rel=canonical' or 'hreflang'), and it is strongest when several such terms co-occur in one passage. The same words in other senses (a matrix's or an officer's 'rank', a missing 'link', a 'meta'-analysis, supply-chain 'optimisation', Google's corporate news), non-search advertising (television, print, email, social), generic web words ('website', 'page', 'hosting', 'stylesheet', 'browser', a plain https URL) and SEO advice reworded without these terms ('climb the results page', 'earn citations') do not fire: the trigger is the search-marketing term itself, not the general idea.

The negative pole fires on the word that takes alternatives out of a proposition the preceding clause has just set up - the exception word 'except', the restrictive focus particle 'only/Only', and the clause-level adversative 'but' - and its strength tracks how strongly that preceding clause establishes the set being restricted. 'except' peaks at 2.5-4.8 when the clause first asserts sameness or near-identity ('the result is the same as before except the name', 4.8; 'almost identical to a regular result set, except that ...', 3.7; the scan's own 'the same as a regular SQL result set, except that ...', 3.0), gives roughly half that after 'different' ('The result is different except the name', 0.9), and only 0.2-1.0 after a plain quantified statement ('All the students passed except John', 0.2; 'Everyone was there except me', 1.0, versus 0.05 for 'with me'); 'only/Only' fires when it restricts a quantity, condition or instrument inside a running sentence ('...advisor, only 6 per cent cited debt', 3.7-4.6; 'Fade out, only if the URL ...', 3.1; 'using only a metre stick', 2.2) but not as an attributive or idiomatic modifier or at the start of a text ('the only map that works', 'if only', 'only just', all at or below 0.15); 'but' fires only as a clause-level contrast, strongest after 'the same ...' ('The same thing happened, but nobody noticed', 2.8) or a first-person/agentive claim about a definite thing ('I like this map, but ...', 2.4-2.6), and is weak after a bare copular property clause ('The map is large, but ...', 0.1). Near-synonyms never fire (excluding, apart from, other than, besides, save for; yet, though, however, although; just, merely, solely), phrasal and correlative uses of 'but' stay at baseline ('everyone but John', 'not X but Y', 'not only ... but also', 'anything but', 'last but not least', 'but for'), the clause after the marker has no effect on the peak (it is already fixed before that clause is read; 'but I found it easy' and 'but I found it difficult' both give exactly 2.394), and the pole's few other fires ('.accept', '$provide', 'if' in Kotlin) are isolated singles at 1.0-1.5 rather than a token family.

The negative pole encodes the mathematical concept of a map/function between two objects: it peaks on the token that carries the correspondence - the arrow in f:X->Y ('\rightarrow', '\to', '\mapsto'), 'maps' plus its preposition ('to', 'onto', 'into'), 'from ... to' once a map or function has been named, 'between' after 'a map', and 'reversed' where a map is inverted - and on the words naming a map or its parts ('function', 'mapping', 'relation', 'range', 'inverse', 'one-to-one', 'image'), strongest when the map's arguments are abstract or symbolically denoted (X, Y, A, B, f, G, H, a vector, the kernel). The same strings outside a correspondence leave it near zero ('he climbed onto the roof', 'the train goes from X to Y', 'the bomb annihilates the city', 'a link between the two spaces', 'encryption converts the message into ciphertext'), as does mathematical prose that states no correspondence ('the polynomial has three real roots', 'the sequence converges uniformly').

Fires on words that denote the authorities taking a person into restraint, i.e. arrest, detention, custody or jail ('arrested', 'under arrest', 'into custody', 'detention'/'détention', 'sent to jail', 'caught'/'apprehended' by police, 'imprisoned'), on the illegality marker 'Unlawful/unlawful', and on the preposition right after such a verb ('arrested for', 'jailed for', 'imprisoned for'). It is weak or silent when the same word has a non-criminal sense ('joint custody', 'the ball was caught', 'in this case', 'a case of beer') and on conviction or sentencing words ('convicted', 'sentenced to', 'prison' all stay below 0.1 of max). It is retrospective: the Jacobian lens suppresses criminal/sentencing tokens rather than promoting the next token.

Fires on a word naming a field of artistic, aesthetic or vernacular culture: design, art, folklore/folk, popular (as in popular culture or vote), costume, opera, sculptor, singers. It fires hardest when the word labels the whole discipline or category ('Cover design by', 'design has become', 'popular culture', 'In folklore') rather than a concrete object, and stays near zero for the same frames filled with non-cultural domains (finance, tax, medicine, price, chemistry, code). Retrospective: the peak is on the culture word itself and is driven mostly by that token and its immediate modifier.

L5/N245+ fires retrospectively on the current token when it realizes a vivid outdoor-adventure scene cue, rugged terrain, snow/surf conditions, or energetic motion phrasing (steep, rocky, crag, ridge, slopes, powder, avalanche, reef, waves, surf, climbed, along, directly), with peak strength 0.5-7+ scaling with cue specificity, spreading to neighboring function words in such passages (e.g. ' the' reaches ~3 before ' steep'), and firing lexically even when the sense is non-outdoor ('surf the web' still fires); outside such passages it shows only a weak <=0.4 background on common temporal/contrastive continuations (year, morning, while, in/of/the, far, three) and stays near-flat (<0.1) on short generic, office/abstract, or calm-domestic sentences. It is retrospective, not lookahead: peaks sit on the cue token itself with local attribution (mean 1.9 tokens back), the Jacobian and logit lenses agree on nothing (overlap 0, kurtosis ~3.3, no coherent promoted set), and ablating it barely moves the next-token distribution (KL ~1e-5).

The negative pole detects the literal armed-conflict / military-force register, and it fires wherever that register is carried by the current token rather than on the war words themselves: its highest peaks are the function word that continues a conflict noun ('the war in ...' 7.6 on ' in', 'the bombing in ...' 4.3, 'the invasion in ...' 3.2, 'troops into ...' 3.9) or a war content word inside such a span ('terror' completing 'war on terror' 9.8, 'Iraqi' 5.7, 'Afghanistan' 6.9, 'airstrikes' 4.0, 'Islamic State' 2.2), so peaks land on prepositions, digits and proper nouns while the token ' war' alone reaches only ~1.4. It stays near zero when the same surface words carry no armed-conflict sense: metaphorical or figurative war ('the trade/price/bidding/class war in Europe' 0.1-0.6, 'a war of words' 1.4), the identical frame with a civilian noun ('the fair/banking/vacation in Europe' 0.0-0.1, 'he sent workers into the country' 0.4, 'the U.S. economy' 0.7), military words not continued by a conflict phrase ('the troops advanced along the road' 0.5, 'the military band', 'the army recruiter', 'Veterans Day' 0.0-0.3), and peacetime defence bureaucracy ('the Department of Defense annual report' 0.6); the positive pole of the same neuron stays near zero throughout this material, so the claim is one-sided.

Retrospective detector that fires on a token marking return to, repetition of, or habitual re-engagement with a previously established place, activity, or service counterpart (return/returned/returning, back, again, repeat, regular), or naming that ongoing enterprise or counterpart (business, client, customer), only when the context establishes the prior occurrence or ongoing relation; the same token for a first-time motion, one-off event, or unrelated sense (travel, once, famous, party, giving) stays quiet.

Retrospective lexical detector for the scraped 'free download' content-farm register (greeting-card, wallpaper, quotes and font pages): activation is an additive lexical ensemble over the register's offer vocabulary - wallpapers, pictures, quotes, wishes, greetings, cards, messages, icons, downloadable, caption - plus greeting headlines ('Happy Birthday', 'Valentines Day') and design/software-asset identifiers (drawable, background, Icon, .support.constraint, FreeType, freeware, stationery), peaking on the offer-nouns themselves (peaks sit ON ' wallpapers'/' quotes'/' greetings' and the 3 following tokens are not a predictable continuation; Jacobian kurtosis 3.2, logit-lens list is noise, and Qwen2.5-0.5B's tied embeddings make the promoted ' Www'/' Wallpaper'/'Tumblr'/' Cute' list mirror the input key, so this is detection, not lookahead). Response grows with local co-occurrence density of those tokens - a bare twelve-noun register list fires 5.3 vs 0.07 for matched household nouns, a single ' wallpapers' in an otherwise mundane sentence 5.0, pure register prose up to ~12, above the corpus's diluted 3.65 max - while lone date words are a weaker offshoot the register amplifies (' day' 1.9-3.2 in mundane prose, ' Morning' 1.3 in news ratings but 6.5 inside good-morning-wishes spam), and the negative pole is the mirror contrast: it fires on encyclopedic/fan-wiki/reference text and promotes code-bracket tokens ('[$', '[arg', '”）') while suppressing exactly the ' Wallpaper'/'Tumblr' cluster.

The pole detects the concept of an electromagnetic field/force rather than its words: it peaks on the head noun of a physics 'field' compound whose modifier names a physical force or quantity ('magnetic field' ~15, 'electric field' ~9, 'gravitational field' ~7.5, 'force field' ~4) and on the vocabulary and people of magnetism and electricity (magnet, coil, wire, flux, charge, current, induction, electromagnetic, tesla, Faraday ~4-9), in Chinese as well as English (磁场 ~13, 电磁 ~3.4). The same surface tokens in everyday senses ('football field' ~0.2, 'field of view' ~0.6, 'field of study' ~0.3, 'electric bill' ~0, 'current affairs' ~0.5, 'pole vault' ~0.1) and non-electromagnetic science (chemistry, biology, astronomy, optics ~0.2) stay near baseline, the pole is retrospective (measure_lookahead is false and peaks sit on the concept token, never one token before a fixed upcoming word), and a weaker offshoot fires on fantasy-magic force language ('magic' ~3.4, 'spell' ~4.5, 'wand' in a wizard frame ~5).

Retrospective collocation-frame detector: the pole fires on a token that is the conventional continuation of the preceding 1-3 tokens (determiner+noun, verb+particle, noun+of, weekday+range, verb+object noun, digit-inside-number/code idiom), with strength scaling with how strongly that left context licenses it; the same token with the licensing left words replaced or reordered drops sharply, while replacing only the following token leaves it unchanged. A separate ~0.06 bias on the sequence-initial token occurs regardless of identity.

L5/N3436- fires on the body-and-clinic vocabulary of health writing - the body-part, symptom and procedure words that fill medical abstracts and case reports (walking/gait, pain, knee, leg, limb, arm, hearing, stimulation, therapy, surgery, patient, care, disease) - and it is strongest inside clinical or scientific prose, where 'Older adults with knee pain walked more slowly than healthy controls' reaches 3.46 of the pole's 4.12 maximum and almost every content word of a PubMed-style gait abstract fires (69 of 307 tokens above 0.5). It is near zero when the same body words appear in sport, cooking, legal, code or conversational prose ('The striker injured his knee...' peaks at 0.34, 'We walked to the park...' at 0.08), near zero on an everyday synonym put in the same clinical slot ('talking' for 'walking', 'ache' for 'pain'), and near zero on the measurement/abstraction words that share the same clinical sentences (extension, strength, joint, acuity, factors); its only non-clinical trigger is a weaker (~0.5 of max) response to the ' (' that opens a parenthetical specification ('Patients (n=123)', 'device (France)').

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a frequent, stereotyped local chunk: a common collocation or template slot made highly predictable by the preceding one or two tokens (e.g. so+fast, submit+your, For+i+in, powerhouse+of+the+cell, According+to+the+X). Strength is set jointly by the filler token and how constraining the local bigram is, so the same token in a rare or unconstrued bigram (slowly after so, garage after powerhouse of the, sentence-initial Your) fires weakly or not at all.

The pole detects R-style data-analysis source code: it peaks (1.5-7, versus <=0.5 elsewhere) on the code-identifier tokens that name R functions and named arguments (c, rep, length, plot, main, col, data.frame, setCellValue, print) and on the punctuation fragments glued to them in call syntax ('(x', "('", "',", '),', ','), including the first token after a '<-' assignment. The same words in ordinary prose ('the plot of the novel', 'the mean value', or 'the c function' with no code frame), English lists, the numeric/string data values inside the code, and Java/JS method-call code stay below the activity threshold; the raw neuron is instead suppressed on the operators and delimiters that precede those identifiers ('<-', 'for', '(') and on identifier continuations ('vals', 'Row', 'CellValue'), which is the contrast its negative pole draws.

This pole detects the terminating token of a code or formal-notation statement in a technical passage: it peaks on whatever closes the statement — the closing bracket/brace/quote of an expression (');', '];', '";', '}'), the ' ='/'<-'/' :=' that finishes a variable name, or the newline/space token that ends a code line — fires hardest on the first such statement after a prose line, and decays across the following lines of an unbroken block (2.6 then 1.8 then 1.2 in a four-line block, restored to 2.7 when prose separates the lines). The same symbols, words and numbers in ordinary prose sit at the floor (about 0.1-0.4, versus 1.5-4.2 here), so it tracks code-form text and expression endings rather than those tokens themselves; the one token-level exception is the arrow ' <-', which also fires on its own inside plain prose (1.3-2.4).

The negative pole is a graded semantic detector for temptation and enticement: it fires hardest on the word that names an allurement or impulse pulling someone toward an action they might resist or yield to — tempt/tempted/tempting/temptation (strength 5–15), urge (5–6), and entice/enticement, seduce/seductive, lure, alluring (2–7) — and, less reliably (1.5–6), on the adjacent vocabulary of yielding to or holding out against that pull (resist, give in, yield, succumb, can't help but, devil, sins, Satan); it is lexical-semantic, not propositional, so a mention fires whether the clause urges, forbids or denies the temptation ('Don't do it — this can be tempting'; 'They are tempted by nothing'). Bare function words, ordinary volition and purpose stay near zero (sentence peaks: 'I want to go' 0.42, 'He needs to go' 0.10, 'They plan to contest the ruling' 0.09, 'John and Mary travelled to Paris in spring' 0.16, 'He sat on the mat' 0.04), the propensity rim (tend, tendency, desire, inclined, attracted, appealing, craving; 0.7–2.7) is not a reliable positive, and a following 'to'/'toward' peaks only when it is the complement of one of these pull words ('we tend to', 'an urge to', 'a tendency to').

The negative pole fires on the token that refers to a periodical publication as an object or institution — the printed newspaper or magazine itself, not its content: strongly (about 3.5-10 of the 9.8 scale) on the periodical nouns newspaper, magazine, tabloid, broadsheet, zine, periodical, and on 'paper' in the morning-paper/newspaper sense, on their equivalents in other languages (Zeitung 6.4, periódico 8.1, quotidien 4.9, giornale 6.5, газета 6.4, 报纸 8.6) and on foreign outlet names (Le Monde 4.2, Haaretz 4.6, Le Parisien 5.8, El Diario 4.6), and, while that frame is active, on its publishing apparatus and cycle (publication/publishing/publisher 3.5-5.2, editor/editorial 3-4.7, circulation 4.3-8.5, issue, edition, 'published monthly', 'delivered twice a day', 'every week'). It stays near zero on news content and newsroom staff (news, article, headline, story, reporter, journalist, columnist, correspondent) and on broadcast/digital media (radio, television, podcast, network, blog, website), and it stays below the 0.25 x scale active threshold on common English mastheads (New York Times, Guardian ~1), on non-periodical senses of the same words (paper as material, issue as topic, press as push, journal as diary, film/photo editor, book/app/music publisher), and on journal, gazette and newsletter (~1-2.4); the peak lands on the concept-bearing token itself (often its final subword), retrospectively, and its Jacobian-lens output promotes the same publication vocabulary but does not prepare a specific upcoming token.

The negative pole fires retrospectively on the subword pieces of words that are not ordinary English vocabulary - rare proper nouns, foreign words and technical coinages ('Kunsthistorisches' 0.71, 'Herengracht' 0.79, 'Goppenstein' 0.74, 'Pullanikkatil' 0.65, invented 'glorpenstein' 0.64) - with the burst spread over every piece of the word and, on average, strongest on its first piece (mean 0.16 first vs 0.12 last across a 60-document rescan); it stays at background on ordinary English words however long or rare ('sesquipedalian' 0.29, 'photosynthesis' 0.24, 'project' 0.24, 'market' 0.29) and is graded by name familiarity ('Albert Einstein' 0.27, 'Barack Obama' 0.33 vs 'Wolfram Burgard' 0.57, 'Deepa Pullanikkatil' 0.64). Numerically it exceeds 0.3 on 12.8% of tokens inside capitalized non-dictionary words against 1.4% inside lowercase dictionary words (about 9x in the tail), is not surprisal-driven (Spearman with token NLL -0.03) or positional (position R^2 0.004), and the few common single-token peaks in the scan ('Arctic', 'glacier', 'Norway', 'snow') belong to the neuron's minor SwiGLU sign regime (g+u-: 3 of 123 tokens above 0.4, versus 120 in the detector regime g-u+), so they are a second, much rarer job; because the Jacobian-lens promoted set is incoherent (kurtosis 4.5, logit-lens overlap 0) and zero-ablating the pole moves the next-token distribution by only KL 2.8e-4, the claim is retrospective, not lookahead.

Pole N4792+ fires retrospectively on the technical register of evidence synthesis and appraisal: it is active on the content words of text that aggregates, grades or vouches for a body of research findings - 'systematic review(s)' (13.5-16.4 on the pole's 16.0 scale), 'meta-analysis' (15.1), 'Cochrane ... systematic reviews' (16.0), 'GRADE' with 'certainty of the evidence' (15.8), a 'PubMed/Medline search' of trials (11.6), 'quality/certainty of the evidence' (11.1), the 'eligible studies' inclusion step of a review (10.5), 'evidence-based' (6.3-7.7), a pooled or 'single estimate' aggregation over studies (6.1-7.2, and 6.4 even when the pooled items are interviews rather than studies), 'moderate evidence that ...' (6.3), 'forty-two studies of the treatment' (6.7-8.4) and 'no strong evidence that ...' (4.9), while 'peer-reviewed' (0.6-3.0), a lone 'evidence', 'review', 'studies' or 'systematic' in ordinary prose, and an isolated description of one study's design ('participants were randomly assigned to the drug or placebo in a double-blind trial', 2.6) stay at 0.4-4.8. It does not fire on the same words in other senses (film/performance review <=0.23, a criminal trial <=0.29, pooled funds 0.00, evidence in court <=0.18), on generic science statements ('research shows', 'scientists discovered', 'Science has shown' <=0.6), or on plain-language paraphrases without the technical terms ('a careful summary of many experiments ... moderately confident' <=3.5); it is topic-independent - the same phrases reach 15-19 in astronomy, education, business and machine-learning text - and ablating the pole removes probability from the same register words ('review', 'systematic', 'meta', 'evidence', 'research', 'study') rather than from one particular upcoming token, so the claim is retrospective.

Retrospective local-licensing detector: the pole fires on the current token when it is the expected continuation of its immediately preceding context, i.e. the second half of an adjacent collocation or syntactic dependency (verb/adjective + preposition or particle as in 'open from', 'calls for', 'hiked to'; verb + complement pronoun as in 'are you', 'chase you'; determiner/adjective + noun as in 'the pan', 'chemical energy', 'three times a day'; proper noun + list or appositive comma as in 'Paris,', 'Tokyo,'; code collocates 'import numpy', 'WHERE active'; subword and tag completions 'Shakespeare', '<body>'). The same surface token without its licensing context ('from' after 'cloudy' collapses 1.093 to 0.0) or a different token in the same licensed slot ('day'->'cat', 'pan'->'dog', 'for'->'yesterday' all collapse to near zero) does not fire, while distant context changes ('museum'->'gallery') leave firing nearly intact.

Fires on the head verb of a clause predicate once its nominal subject has been read: finite copula/auxiliary/modal (is, was, are, been, can, should, did) or finite lexical verb (divide, exert, resulted, makes). Same verb form as a noun, imperative without subject, or non-finite fragment drives it weakly.

Retrospective detector that peaks on the word completing a conventionalized multi-word technical or jargon collocation (anatomical, clinical, laboratory, sports-code, news-reporting, or code formula such as cruciate ligament, hip flexor, TSBV agar, laboratory tests, terror-related attacks); the same word in a non-formulaic everyday frame activates substantially less.

The pole fires on the non-initial subword pieces of words that fall outside the model's ordinary English vocabulary: foreign-language words and foreign personal or place names that the tokenizer has to spell out over several pieces (Ehsan, Zohoori, Tarmizi, Abdelakim, Jaafar, McLeod, Srinivasan, Podlaskie Voivodeship, Ouagadougou, forhåndsvarsel, Der Schauspieldirektor), with the peak landing on a middle or final piece of the word rather than its first piece. It stays near zero on ordinary English words, on rare technical and scientific English vocabulary (morbidity, malignancies, nephron, epithelial, methylphenidate, histopathology), and on Western names and places the model already holds as single tokens (Smith, Miller, Springfield, Paris, London).

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes a lexicalized multi-token chunk: a subword piece finishing a split (usually technical or rare) word (Richt+er, seism+icity, megaw+att, pre+term, myd+ri+asis, Apog+ee, f+ission, cord+ite, norm+ative, U++) or the second word of a fixed collocation (Family+planning, low+fertility, sea+ice, seismic+waves, domestic+energy, X+-linked), i.e. when the current token is strongly cued by the immediately preceding 1-2 tokens. Near-miss: the identical tail token after a non-cueing prefix (careful+planning 0.02, sea+spray, Family+dinner) or the same stem as a merged single token stays near zero; acknowledged leftovers are a weak transit-noun offshoot (station/platform ~0.5, amplified by rail-topic long context) and the scan's generic we+can peak, which does not replicate in isolation.

The negative pole is a detector for the written name of a computer program in a technical passage: it fires on the token that spells a compiler, interpreter or command-line utility (gcc, clang, curl, kubectl, ffmpeg, vim, java, python, ssh, scp, grep, sed, awk, pdflatex, mencoder, rubocop, MSVC, fc-list, wine), including whichever subword piece the name is split into (the 'ex' of pdflatex, the 'VC' of MSVC, the 'ocop' of rubocop, the '-list' of fc-list). It is a program-name detector rather than a computing-topic detector: putting an ordinary or generic word in the same slot (compiler, tool, soap, query, notes, agent) drops the peak to 0.2-0.9, computing prose that names no program stays below 1 (threshold 1.47), plain narrative prose stays below 0.5, and generic system words such as make, git and docker are much weaker than distinctive tool names.

This pole's negative-pole strength tracks a feminine-marked noun phrase in non-English text: it peaks on the token immediately after a feminine determiner - Spanish la/una/esta/toda/las/esa/aquella/alguna/varias/otras, Italian-French la, German die - and carries into the rest of the phrase (la puerta 2.9, las puertas 3.1, la Diversidad 5.0, Las Baulas 1.8, la strada 3.4, la boulangerie 4.3, Anoche la luna brillaba 2.5), while the same words after a masculine (el, un, este, todo, los, ese, aquel, muchos, otros, il, der, le), gender-neutral (mi, su, cada) or English (the, a) determiner, or a Spanish word quoted inside English ('the word puerta'), stay at or below 0.3. The noun's own gender and meaning do not matter ('la zorblat' 2.5 vs 'el zorblat' 0.06, 'la casa' vs 'el casa'), and the sub-threshold activations on English names, acronyms and feminine words (Rolls-Royce 1.2, ILO 0.8, SIM 0.6, she/her ~0.3) are an offshoot that this rule does not cover.

This pole fires on measurement-unit words (degrees, Celsius/Fahrenheit, cups, mg, liters, volts) when they function as units quantifying something; the same word forms used as ordinary objects (drinking cups, academic degrees) and non-unit nouns after a number (cars, bricks) evoke little or nothing, and strength is graded by the surrounding measure context rather than by an explicit numeral.

This pole fires on a token that completes a tight, overlearned local dependency with the immediately preceding head: a licensed verb complement or particle ('stared at' but not 'resembled at' or 'shouted at'; 'pleaded guilty'; quoted 'are you'), a familiar modifier-head or fixed-phrase completion ('the cold', 'on average', 'upon a time'), with strength graded by how strongly that head licenses the continuation. It does not explain why a surprising noun ('potatoes', 0.200) out-fires the predictable pronoun ('it', 0.067) as object of affirmative 'can believe'.

The negative pole fires on a word asserting that a thing, property or quantity is absent or zero: the negative determiner 'no' in a predicate noun phrase ('there is/are/was/were no X', 'has/had no X', 'with no X', 'found/showed/contains no X'), zero-value words ('null', 'undefined', 'None', 'none', 'nil', 'zero', 'Off'), zero-price 'free', privative words ('-less', 'unavailable', 'absent', 'omitted', 'extinct', 'missing', 'lack', 'without', 'devoid', 'waived', 'exempt') and negated existence ('does not exist', 'if (!x)'), reaching 0.8-3.5 (up to 5.2 on 'waived') against the 1.06 active threshold (0.25 x the scan max of 4.23). It is not sentential negation or a generic negative-polarity detector: 'not', 'never' and "don't" stay at or below about 0.5, as do the discourse answer 'No.', 'No.' meaning 'number', container-state 'empty'/'blank'/'full', sentence-initial 'No X' subjects, and every affirmative counterpart ('there is some water', 'the fee is charged').

Fires retrospectively on words denoting internal operational components or organs of physical devices and anatomical systems (such as mechanical/electrical working parts like alternator, filament, fuse, relay, piston, pump, and visceral organs like kidney, stomach, colon), as well as thermodynamic phase changes (e.g., boils) and expressions of capacity or inability (e.g., can't, cannot). It remains inactive on external body parts, everyday furniture, abstract concepts, and non-capacity modal verbs.

This pole fires on the formatting skeleton of laid-out, non-narrative text: whitespace/layout tokens (blank lines, indentation runs and newline runs at the end of centred caption, cover-sheet and signature lines in court filings) and delimiter or notation punctuation that opens or glues a structured payload (markup `[](`, code `{`, `['`, `('`, URI/path pieces such as `.org`, `/v`, `-packages`), plus the low-content identifier fragments of that notation (`provide`, `exports`, `packages`, ` sp`, ` alpha`, ` for` inside a counsel-of-record line), while ~89% of its 209 strongest scan tokens are pure punctuation or whitespace tokens. The same punctuation, whitespace or words inside running prose stay inactive (prose paragraph breaks peak at 0.08-0.16 against 1.3-2.2 for the identically-worded indented court header; prose 'provide' 0.06 against 1.48 in code; prose ' for' 0.00 against 0.61-0.74 in a counsel listing), so its activity marks 'this position belongs to the form/format layer of a formatted document or source code', not the lexical content (its negative pole instead peaks on open-class content words such as 'code', 'Diseases' and 'scored').

Fires on the word that says a just-mentioned cause, tool or action makes some outcome possible: enabling verbs used causatively ('enable(s)/enabling', 'allow(s)/allowing', 'permit(s)', 'let(s)', 'help(s)', 'facilitate', French 'permettre'), the means connective 'That/This way', 'makes it possible', and purpose 'to' after a means ('use cookies to'). It stays near zero on non-enabling verbs in the same slot (improve, prevent, require, force), on nominal or imperative uses ('the permit', 'Allow me'), and on literal 'way' ('the long way home').

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a familiar, lexically specific two-token pairing cued by the immediately preceding word (e.g. interest->rates, river->flooded, played->the, Please->remember, time->there), collapsing toward zero when the same peak token follows a cue word that breaks the pairing, and it stays near-silent on sentence-boundary tokens such as final '.' and sentence-initial 'The'. An acknowledged exception is that some adjectives (e.g. 'purple') drive strong activation after determiners regardless of pairing familiarity, so the pairing account does not cover every peak.

Retrospective detector for feminine reference at or just after the current token: it fires when the peak token itself is a feminine-marked word (pronoun she/her/herself, female proper name such as Marie, feminine role noun such as princess/girls/women) or the word immediately continuing a feminine-subject clause; masculine counterparts and gender-neutral words stay near baseline.

The negative pole fires on the token of a content noun that names a specialised, domain-specific kind of thing: lodging and travel (hotel, motel, inn, resort, hostel, lodge, cabin, guesthouse, campground, tent, airport), diplomacy (embassy, consulate, visa), genetics/medicine (allele, genotype, phenotype, chromosome, genome, virus, pathogen, fossil, and 'injury' only inside a clinical frame), vehicle/tech brands (Jeep, Toyota, Hyundai, Lenovo, Ryzen) and procurement (bid, offer). It is silent on everyday-object and generic-place nouns (table, chair, door, museum, castle, station) and on the same words used in an everyday or narrative sense ('players with a head injury', 'the digital divide'), and its peaks sit on the token where a domain term is completed: the final fragment of a multi-token domain word or number (…ogen in 'pathogen', …vention in 'convention', …site in 'campsite', the last digits of '6.2', '4000', 'F1') or the whole-word token in informative prose that is about that domain.

The negative pole detects the head of a clause-level circumstance adjunct from a small set — 'with', 'once' and the compound 'now that' — firing where that head is complete: on 'with' when it sits at a clause's left edge (sentence-initial after a full stop, newline or semicolon, or after a coordinator such as 'and'/'but' or the complementizer 'that'), on 'once' when it heads a clause (fronted or trailing, including sentence-initial idioms like 'Once again'), and on the 'that' of clause-initial 'now that'. The same words inside a clause are near zero — 'with' as a verb complement, NP-internal modifier, postposed or parenthetical with-phrase; 'once' as a clause-internal frequency adverb — as are other clause-initial prepositions and subordinators (in, at, by, for, after, when, if, because, although, while), which stay below the active threshold.

Retrospective detector for noun phrases naming support roles, service departments, facilities, or equipment that an institution provides to its members (e.g. chaplains, counsellors, financial-aid advisors, Human Resources, washrooms, meals, busses, generators, radios), typically peaking at the completion of the compound; strength is boosted when the surrounding passage describes the institution providing, inspecting, or maintaining them, consistent with its staff/logistics output direction and heavy long-range attribution.

This pole fires retrospectively on the function word that opens a predicative complement discharging a complement-taking head already read: a shell noun (knack, way, sequence), a catenative or reportive verb (manage, make sure, convinced, believe), or a long fronted scene-setting adjunct closed by a comma. The same function word (for, to, is, sure, comma) stays quiet when the licensing head is replaced or the long setup is absent.

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a binary paired frame opened within the previous ~6 tokens: a from->to range endpoint, a change-of-state verb->into complement, or the separator/second item of a two-element formal pair (numeric tuple, column list, argument list, coordinator), with weaker firing on determiner->noun and similar head-complement completions. The same token stays near-silent without its opener (purpose-'to', 'into' after a non-conversion verb, comma outside a pair), and swapping the frame's content leaves firing unchanged.

Retrospective detector with two narrow jobs: (a) it fires on verse-presenting or verse-analyzing text — the words lyrics/lyric/poem(s)/sonnet/verse, a poet-songwriter surname completing a full name, or a colon-plus-blank-line — only when the context presents, quotes, or structurally analyzes verse (published poems, lyric sheets, a labeled verse followed by a quoted line, discussion of a sonnet's turn); and (b) it fires on short fixed alphanumeric literals in formal syntax — a sha384/sha512 digest fragment inside an integrity attribute or a single short exponent/limit term (x^2, n^{-1}) in math/HTML markup. It stays weak or inactive for a bare indefinite 'a poem' in a school-task sentence, a musician name in non-verse recording-studio prose, long compositional sum-plus-fraction identities, and the same digest/formula strings in plain prose.

Fires selectively on desiderative and intentional control verbs ('hopes', 'wishes', 'wants', 'desires') when embedded in object relative clauses and object extraction contexts with an infinitive complement. It remains inactive on non-volitive control verbs, subject-extracted relatives, and canonical clauses, though weak background activations (0.2–0.45) occur on prepositions and clause boundaries due to the SwiGLU double-negative (g-u-) regime.

Fires on the digit that starts the numeric payload of a character escape the model has to decode rather than read as a word: the first digit after an HTML character-reference prefix (. -> 2.0, ' -> 1.2, all ten digits fire equally after '&#'), the hex digits of a \uXXXX escape (\u00e0 -> 1.0), and the digits of %XX percent-escapes inside an already-encoded string such as a URL (retURL=%2Fa0r%2Fo -> 1.4). It stays at or below zero on ordinary words, on plain numerals outside an escape (which drive the opposite pole), and on named entities such as & or  .

The positive pole detects the speaker/writer's own deictic self-reference: it fires on the first-person pronoun tokens ' I', 'I', ' me', ' my', 'My', ' we', 'We', ' us', ' our', 'Our' (with first-person contractions such as 'm/'ll/'ve and cross-lingual equivalents 'nous', 'notre', 'mi', 'Vi'), and sits at its floor on second- and third-person pronouns (you/he/him/his/they/them/their, 0.0-0.5 in the same frames) and on 'I' inside a technical identifier (IGF-I, I2C, IIC, at or below 0). Within first-person pronouns the strength separates an utterance put to a hearer from narration: appeals, apologies, corrections, self-justifying questions and quoted dialogue clear the activity line ('forgive me for...' 6.06, 'correct me if I...' 6.37, 'don't get me wrong' 3.66, 'What did I do wrong?' 4.72, 'the trouble I have caused you' 3.50, 'Do we know you at all?' 2.76, against 2.87 / 2.86 / 0.50 / 0.43 / 0.15 / 0.10 when only the pronoun's person changes; the bare 'forgive X for' and 'correct X if' frames keep a residual near 2.9 whatever the person), whereas first-person pronouns in plain third-person narration stay far below it ('the meeting ended early, and I walked home alone' 0.88, 'the report said that I had missed the deadline' 0.94).

The pole fires on a hand-held implement - a tool, weapon, musical instrument, eating or writing implement, or portable device - presented as an object in a person's hands: it peaks on the implement noun itself (chisel, hammer, rifle, camera, knife, guitar, wrench), is strongest with grip and manipulation verbs (grip, swing, pick up, carry, raise, clean, holster) and weakest when the same noun is only mentioned, owned or banned. It falls to baseline for non-implement graspables in identical frames (food, rope, stones, boxes, clothing), furniture and abstract nouns, stays sub-threshold for vehicles and machines even when operated, and fires at roughly half strength on the third-person possessive that introduces a handled object ('picked up his ...', 'raising his/her ...') even when that object is not an implement.

Retrospective: the pole fires at the onset of a main clause that resumes after a fronted dependent element (a participial phrase, prepositional phrase, if/when-clause or appositive) that closes just before the peak, usually at a comma but often without one, and it peaks on the resumed clause's opening auxiliary/modal/wh-word or subject pronoun (' could', ' would', ' can', ' may', ' what', ' who', ' is', ' I', ' we', ' has', "'ve") or its first predicate word (' possible', ' suggest', ' critical'); the fronted element can be as short as two tokens and long prefaces neither help nor hurt (measured delta -0.02), so the pole is not context-length dependent. Firing is strongest when the resumed clause is a question, request, suggestion, or possibility/obligation/evaluation statement ('could you please', 'is it possible to', 'I suggest', 'it is critical that'); the same tokens continuing rather than resuming a clause (embedded 'what', mid-clause 'would', object 'I'), coordination and serial-list commas, sentence-starting clauses with no fronted element, and code/escape text all stay near zero, and the Jacobian lens is flat (kurtosis 3.5, agreement 0%) with a suppressed list of backslash/escape tokens that exactly mirrors the negative pole's promoted list, so this is a prose clause-resumption feature, not a lookahead or code-region unit.
