Qwen2.5-0.5B L7/N4085+ responds to the noun that names a counted or named division of a larger ordered whole - a slot/position inside a document, series, table, building, administrative geography or time axis (chapter, page, paragraph, stanza, verse, section, line, column, row, layer, season, episode, act, round, floor, street, province, district, quarter, year, Friday) - and, when an index identifies the slot, to the index token that completes the phrase too ('In chapter seven' peaks 1.94 on ' seven'; 'the third page of the book' peaks 3.07 on ' of'; 'season one' peaks 3.00 on ' one'). The class is semantic and graded rather than a token list or a part-of-whole relation: held-out members fire (paragraph 1.99, stanza 1.71, column 1.22, page 3.01) while everyday concrete nouns in the identical grammatical slot (sandwich 0.00, blanket 0.02, pumpkin 0.00, door 0.00, peach, basket), generic part-whole words (roof 0.44, handle 0.01, middle 0.08, capital 0.00, part 0.19) and the same words in a non-structural sense ('Season the chicken' 0.04, 'we must act' 0.00, 'fishing line' 0.14, 'page at the hotel' 0.15) stay near the 0.03-0.16 baseline, and the containing whole is irrelevant ('line of the poem' and 'line of the menu' both peak 2.45).

Fires on an adverbial means/manner/circumstance preposition attached to a preceding verb phrase ('with', 'by', 'through', 'using', 'via'; e.g. 'lowball me with', 'outscored all opponents by', 'woke me with', 'mitigated through', sentence-initial 'By using/By payment') and peaks on that preposition or on the first token of its object (usually the determiner/possessive 'a/an/their/his', a number, or a gerund). It stays near zero for the same words in other roles (comitative 'came with a friend', noun-modifying 'the woman with a red hat', passive agent 'written by a famous author') and for non-means prepositions in the same slot ('about', 'for', 'of', 'in', 'at', 'after'). A separate leftover: it also fires strongly on the token ')\n' that closes a legal citation year like '646 (2001)' followed directly by a newline.

This pole is a broad, graded retrospective dial that separates third-person description of physical or technical subject matter from person-directed advice and service prose: it is active throughout passages that describe objects, machines, vehicles, plants, materials, quantities or technical processes (tempered glass and windshields, five-axle trucks and aero engines, garden soil and seeds, binary arithmetic and calculus, aircraft history, gene expression in plants), and it is consistently near zero in advice or service prose addressed to the reader about health, safety, education or feelings (anxiety and depression, exercising for mood, yoga, language courses, N95 masks, emergency alerts, essay-writing services). It is a graded dial, not a fixed-token, positional, frequency or surprisal detector - 52% of mid-sequence tokens are exactly 0 and its weights promote no coherent token set (Jacobian kurtosis 3.4) - apart from one sequence-start artifact: the scan's single strongest activation (1.42) sits at the second token of an input, depends only on the first two tokens, and occurs that strongly in about 18% of scan windows.

The negative pole fires on the function word at which a partitive quantity phrase hands over to the definite thing being measured: ' of' when it follows a numeral, an indefinite quantifier or a quantity/realisation noun ('two of the drives', '13 of the drives', 'several of the drivers', 'an older version of the driver', 'a sample of the mixture'), and, most strongly, the ' the' that follows such an ' of' when the head is a substance-amount noun (concentration, amount, quantity, volume, sample, presence, mixture, solution, mass - e.g. 'a high concentration of the powder', 'a large amount of the liquid', 'the presence of the tumour'). It is near zero on the same two tokens everywhere else: after property or ratio nouns ('the colour / temperature / name / purpose / position of the powder', 'a large proportion / fraction / share / part of the powder'), after definite-set quantifiers ('most / all / half / none of the'), and on ' the' in ordinary definite noun phrases ('store the drives in the cabinet', 'the first', 'the most').

Fires on the metalinguistic naming-and-origin frame: the tokens of an expression that ties a thing to the name it carries and says where that name comes from or is given after, as in 'X is named after/for Y', 'X takes its name from Y', 'the name comes from Y', 'the name given/attributed/applied to Y', 'hence the name'. The peak lands on the naming word itself ('name', 'named', 'renamed') or on the preposition just after it ('after', 'for', 'of', 'from'), and stays near zero where those same words occur without the designation ('his name is John', 'he wrote his name on the paper', 'named in the lawsuit', 'after the storm'); a weaker, uncovered residue remains on document labels such as 'References' and code identifiers such as 'import_module'.

The pole fires, retrospectively, on a punctuation or symbol token used as reference/typographic apparatus rather than as running-prose punctuation: most reliably the period closing a citation or reference abbreviation ('p.', 'pp.', 'pg.', 'para.', 'ch.', and the same mark in 'p. 34', 'pp. 34-37', 'fn. 3', 'Jan. 22'), a quotation mark detached from the quoted words by a space (" ' the priory ' "), and an exclamation mark ending a command inside a list of commands ('Read! Listen! Write!'), as opposed to an ordinary exclamation ('Wow! ...'). It does not fire on normally set prose punctuation (a sentence-final period, commas, question marks, colons, semicolons, decimal points, quotes attached to their words) nor on the spelled-out equivalents ('page 34', 'paragraph 34', 'Read, Listen, Write'), and a bare hyphen, slash, dash, ellipsis or '>>>' raises it only when the preceding fifty or so tokens already carry several such marks.

Retrospective detector of a stated age of a particular person: it peaks on the token that completes the age phrase - 'old' in 'N-year-old' or 'N years old', the numeral of 'aged N' / 'at age N', and the digits of a bare appositive age ('Name, 60,'). It stays near zero when the same forms describe a non-person or are generic ('the tree was 56 years old', 'men aged 44', '56-page', 'at mile 80'); a weaker (0.5-2) response also occurs on the 'of/from <place or institution>' appositive that identifies a named person ('First Last, of Springfield').

This pole detects formulaic, stored text rather than composed prose: it peaks on the token where a memorized or repeated formula is recognised - the opening tokens of successive items of a packed QA/math-dataset list ('What is the greatest common divisor of', 'Calculate', 'Is', 'Does'), the attribution line of a licence/copyright header ('...and contributors.', 'The Chromium Authors'), and a small set of stock web strings ('We use cookies', 'You can unsubscribe at any time', 'Please enter your...'). It stays inactive for the same words in ordinary sentences and one-off questions, and for generic boilerplate that lacks those exact formulas ('All rights reserved', 'Powered by WordPress').

This pole fires when the current token continues an already-open phrase or clause (determiner/adjective to noun, noun to complement or preposition, verb to complement or adverb, stem to suffix, number to unit, keyword to identifier), with strength boosted by a longer same-clause preamble; it stays near zero on tokens that open a new constituent (sentence-initial words, finite main verbs after subjects) and on boundaries such as '.' and 'not', even for otherwise-activating tokens.

The pole fires on a human or institutional reference that is a party to a relation or attribution rather than a bare topic: the object or complement of a contact, speech, meeting or reporting verb or preposition ('interviewed the engineer', 'spoke with the pilot', 'quoted the nurse', 'According to a source close to the family'), or a role/title/kinship reference being introduced or identified together with a name or description ('said co-author Jeff MacInnes', 'lead researcher Benjamin Lok', 'the nurse, a former colleague', 'the author of the study'). It stays inactive when the same person noun is a plain subject/agent or predicate nominal of a simple clause ('The engineer arrived', 'She is a doctor'), when the person is only the topic of a statement or management verb ('described/praised/hired the engineer'), and when the phrase is a bare role noun with a generic place or group complement ('the mayor of the city arrived', 'a member of the committee said').

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a conventional local 2-4-token chunk licensed by the immediately preceding tokens (number plus unit or abbreviation, object plus code attribute, list prefix plus separator or final item, conditional antecedent plus then or until, verb or preposition plus its canonical complement), with strength set jointly by the peak token and its 1-2 predecessors; the same surface token outside such a licensing chunk activates weakly or not at all.

The pole fires retrospectively when the just-read token completes a locally highly predictable multi-token collocation or formulaic phrase (the token is strongly constrained by the preceding 1-3 tokens, e.g. 'average' in 'on average', 'with' in 'compared with', 'cities' in 'capital cities', 'energy' in 'chemical energy', 'not' in 'pleaded not', 'numpy' after 'import', or a determiner directly after a preposition). The same surface token outside its constraining context activates it weakly or not at all.

The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the relator of a transfer-or-subjection predication in formal prose: it fires on the verb that puts a theme through a process, into a new state, or under an authority ('assigned' 1.31, 'randomized' 1.59, 'subjected' 0.85, 'underwent' 0.98, 'transferred' 0.65, 'converted' 0.60, 'tested' 0.50, 'distributed' 0.49, 'undergo' 1.52; everyday manipulation verbs stay down - 'washed' 0.09, 'measured' 0.09, 'counted' 0.04) and, more strongly, on the directional preposition that introduces that predicate's goal, regime or medium ('to' 2.41 in 'assign the samples to groups', 'into' 1.02 in 'transformed the data into insights', 'under' 1.15 in 'distributed under the license', 'through' 1.42 in 'pass it through a hash', Spanish 'en' 1.71 in 'convertir ... en un valor primitivo'). It sits at the floor when those same prepositions are infinitival, static or agentive ('I want to go home' 0.00, 'walk into the room' 0.01, 'the cat is under the table' 0.15, 'assign the samples in groups' 0.54 versus 'to groups' 2.41), so neither the token nor the preposition alone carries it; the negative pole is far sparser (84 versus 498 tokens above a quarter of its max) and peaks on static-description predicates ('define' 2.55, 'surrounds' 1.96, 'includes' 1.02), which I read as the complementary sense but have not audited separately.

This pole fires at the moment a simple declarative clause becomes locally complete: it peaks on the finite past-tense verb, copula or auxiliary that completes an overt definite, pronominal or proper-name subject (court ruled, cat sat, France is, he asked), and on the punctuation, conjunction, complementizer or preposition that immediately continues or closes such a completed verb phrase or noun phrase (door and, valley after, images of, charges .). The same surface token stays quiet when the subject is missing, determinerless or broken, or when the predicate verb is nonfinite.

The pole fires on abstract predication in running prose: the peak lands on a property or assessment noun that heads an 'of' complement ('the value of the building' 1.95 of the scan scale; 'importance of' averages 0.62 over the scan against 0.04 for 'part of' and 0.00-0.04 for 'rest/type/form of'), on verbs of saying, thinking and assessing ('reported' 2.07, 'questioned' 1.61, 'examined' 1.55, 'noted' 1.39, 'discussed' 1.09), on predicative adjectives before their complement ('proud of' 1.08, 'aware of' 0.89), on the connective that introduces such a complement ('of', 'to', 'that', 'by', 'in'), and on wh-complementizers, which beat plain 'that' in the same slot ('discussed whether' 1.20 vs 'discussed that' 0.79; 'whether' averages 0.44 over the scan). It stays near zero on concrete part-whole and partitive 'of' ('the roof of the house' 0.26, 'part of' 0.04, 'rest of' 0.00, 'kind of' 0.04, 'type of' 0.00), on physical action and motion verbs in the same frames ('carried' 0.44, 'threw' 0.39, 'cooked' 0.44, 'walked' 0.33) and on quantity adjectives ('full of' 0.28); about a quarter of its top-20 scan peaks instead fall on sub-word pieces and formatting punctuation in captions and labels ('ED' in 'JUST WATCHED', the ':' of 'Table 9:'), which this account does not cover.

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token supplies the exact value, unit, degree or intensity, frequency, polarity, or identity that resolves a preceding quantitative, gradable, or otherwise open slot (how much, how many, of what, which one, what outcome), responding most strongly to large or intensified specifications and weakly to hedged or vague ones.

This pole is a subject-verb number-agreement detector: it fires on the token carrying a third-person-singular form - a 3sg finite verb (is, was, has, does, or -s forms such as works, explains, drops) or the 3sg possessive 'its' - when that form's grammatical subject/antecedent is plural, including across intervening material or a relative pronoun ('The keys to the cabinet is' peaks at 'is' while 'The key to the cabinets is' does not; irregular plurals such as children/mice/women and invariant nouns the model represents as plural, such as fish/sheep/police, also fire). It stays inactive when the singular form agrees with a singular subject, when the verb is plural/past/bare after a plural subject, when the singular form is inverted before its subject, and when a plural noun is only a nearby non-subject; a plural verb with a singular subject ('The cat are outside') does not fire either, because the 3sg-marked form is required.

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes or continues an already-opened local constituent: the closing bracket or punctuation that ends a call, tag, query, or complete sentence, or the verb, copula, light noun, or function word (are, began, year, of, the) that supplies the expected continuation of a pending subject, list, or prepositional phrase, integrating the preceding ~2-8 tokens. The same surface token in isolation, at a clause onset, or in a fragment without that pending constituent stays weak.

This pole fires on the token that completes a familiar multi-token frame given the preceding context: first-person possessive 'my' after 'for'/'of' and intensifier 'own' after 'my', a particle finishing a common phrasal verb ('into' after 'looking', 'out' after 'reaching'), a function word finishing an institutional or boilerplate name ('COURT' after 'UNITED STATES', 'of' in 'Court of Appeals', the newline ending a patent 'Field of the Invention' heading), or the leading '1' of a multi-digit quantity in structured code/math text. The same surface token with the frame broken, or outside such a frame, activates weakly or not at all.

The positive pole fires on a plural noun that names something each member of a set possesses or exhibits individually - the distributive-possession reading: personal attributes and belongings ('their homes', 'very harsh childhoods', 'criminal pasts', 'their bags/coats/lunches', 'the heads of the patient') and per-item properties ('the sizes of the images', 'brief histories of the properties', fluorescence 'intensities'). It peaks on the plural noun itself (or on its plural suffix token when BPE splits the word, e.g. 'hometown'+'s' at 3.99), is boosted when a plural possessor scopes the noun ('their/our/children's + plural noun', 'the Xs of the Ys', and the distributive markers 'own' and 'themselves'), and falls to near zero (0.03-0.7) on the singular of the same noun, on plurals of generic objects in unpossessed position ('the chairs', 'tables', 'boxes', 'trucks'), on plural person nouns ('parents', 'teachers', 'students'), on irregular plurals used as plain subjects ('children', 'people', 'men'), and on singular nouns that merely end in -s ('bus', 'glass', 'analysis'). The negative pole stays near zero on the same inputs, and the transported output direction promotes the plural/distributive pronouns and quantifiers ('Their', 'their', '各自', '各', '他们的') that are the vocabulary of this feature.

The pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes a locally constraining collocation or grammatical construction projected by the preceding 2-5 tokens (e.g. adjective+noun such as 'final note' or 'negative charge', verb+manner-adverb such as 'fell sharply', verb+particle+intensifier such as 'went by so', preposition/determiner continuations such as 'stored in' or 'submit your'); peak strength is graded by collocational fit, and the same word is silent without its licensing left context or when the filler violates the projected slot.

The negative pole is a sparse rare-name reader: it peaks on a single piece of an uncommon, non-compositional lexical item - a capitalised name the tokenizer splits into several pieces (Jodrell 'rell' 0.81, Merian 'ian' 0.82, Cocos 'ocos' 0.62, Antikythera 'ther' 0.68, Rahmstorf 'm' 0.96 with 'orf' 0.30, Zwicky 'icky' 0.50), an acronym or code (JPL 'PL' 0.83, PROBA-V 'BA' 0.56, ALOS 'LOS' 0.46, GLP-1 'P' 0.71) or a digit/hyphen string (10.3389 '9' 1.14, '-0700' '7' 0.68, 41.73N 'N' 0.67), while ordinary words and familiar single-token names stay at background (Dickens 0.06, London 0.00, Smith 0.04) and the same piece token stays silent inside a common word ('rell' 0.81 in Jodrell but 0.00 in Morrell), so the trigger is the whole rare word being spelled out, not the piece. The detector is graded and word-specific - on a fresh 500-document pass of the scan corpus a multi-piece capitalised word reached 0.4 in 1.16% of its occurrences versus 0.02% for single-token lowercase tokens, yet only ~1% of such words fire and many rare names stay silent (Wolverhampton 0.06, Kidderminster 0.10, Grangemouth 0.06) - and it is neither a surprisal nor a position detector (peak tokens are forced completions with surprisal ~0 and rho = -0.07 against surprisal; position r2 = 0.004), with an incoherent promoted-token set (Jacobian kurtosis 3.5, logit/Jacobian overlap 0) and a zero-ablation KL of 1.3e-4 on peak prompts, so the claim is retrospective.

Retrospective detector of a token that names a place or a people: country, city, region and continent names plus their nationality/ethnicity/language adjectives fire on the mention itself in a neutral text frame (' China' 1.08, ' Dutch' 1.18, ' Egypt' 1.01, ' Japanese' 1.25, ' Scandinavia' 1.00, ' Catalonia' 0.97, ' Mexico' 0.96 of the 2.35 max), including the final piece of a multi-token name ('op' in Ethiopians 1.58, 'anks' in Franks 0.96, ' Lakes' 1.09). The response is graded: it is roughly half strength on other highly specific concrete referents (food plants, animals, medical/technical terms - ' gluten' 1.70, 'bean' in soybean 1.60, ' strawberry' 0.87) and near background on person names (' Mozart' 0.61 vs ' Mexico' 0.86 in the same frame), organisations, everyday objects and abstract nouns (' cup' 0.00, ' table' 0.00, ' idea' 0.04 mean over the scan; chromium 0.33, enzyme -0.37, catechism 0.06, fertile 0.14 in matched frames), so rarity, word length and capitalisation alone do not explain it.

The pole fires on the word that opens a two-part lexical unit the model is completing: the modifier of a noun compound ('tennis shoes', 'credit card', 'confidence interval', 'tax return', 'security guard', 'traffic lights', 'school bus', 'park gate', 'unemployment report'), the first word of a fixed phrase ('greater than', 'at least', 'Where are', 'there lived', 'of the cell'), or the opening fragment of a word split over several tokens ('pro|tons', 'baş|kan', 'immun|oglobulin', 'verkiezing|sprogram'). The peak sits on that opening word, while the word that completes the same unit stays at zero or below it ('shoes' 0.01, 'interval' 0.00, 'tape' -0.12, 'forests' -0.27, 'report' 0.03); it also gives a weaker response (roughly a tenth to a half of the scan's scale) on the first word of common function-word phrases ('of the', 'at least', 'Where are'), and it is inert at a sentence's opening determiner, on digits, punctuation, and code or URL markup.

The pole fires, retrospectively, on the joint where a stance predicate hands over to the material it governs: the complement or reason marker that follows a predicate of desire, ability, necessity or feeling ('wanted to', 'would like to', 'had to', 'able/unable to', 'hard/difficult to', 'due to', 'hoped for', 'delighted/glad/excited to', 'frustrated/sad/bummed because', 'since'), and the predicate token itself, with past-tense, reported forms much stronger than present-tense ones ('I wanted to' 0.99 at ' wanted' versus 0.29 for 'I want to'). The same joint fires inside formulaic records whose next value is fixed by convention rather than composed - the page number of a reporter citation ('472 U.S. 511'), the next field of a timestamp ('08:28:43'), a stack frame's '<module>' - while plain narration of events and generic description ('I wrote a new worship song', 'the cat sat on the mat') stay at zero.

The pole fires on a preposition (mostly ' at' or ' on', also ' for', ' as' (and the article after it), ' under', ' by') that opens a second, different-role adjunct of the clause directly after a finished PP of place, population or audience whose object is a closed referent: a 'City, Region' name pair ('He died in Portland, Oregon at age 71' 1.22, 'born in Monterrey, Mexico on 12 May' 1.11, 'met his wife in Dublin, Ireland at a wedding' 1.03), a 'for <people> with <condition>' description followed by a street address ('a hostel for teenagers with mental health problems at 41 Station Road' 1.59, 'a shelter for men with ... problems at 149 W.' 2.4), a coordinated group of test subjects ('tested in dogs and monkeys for heart toxicity' 1.08) or web pages ('cookies record your activity on our websites for marketing purposes' 1.80); a name pair, coordination or parenthetical in that closed PP multiplies strength 2-8x over a bare common noun ('died in the quiet house at age 71' 0.15, 'tested in the laboratory for' 0.24). It stays below ~0.4 when the same preposition comes straight after the verb or its direct object (so moving the adjunct before the place PP kills it: 'died at age 71 in Portland, Oregon' 0.41 on the later ' in'; 'tested for heart toxicity in dogs' 0.12), after a PP whose object is a bare common noun, on ordinary noun-modifying PP chains ('the Gulf of Mexico', 'the shore of the lake', 'through the sealed port under', all < 0.2), after verbs like 'looked at', and when the closed name ends the sentence ('He moved to Denver, Colorado.' 0.14); ' in <year>' after a name pair is weaker (0.2-0.8) than ' at'/' on'.

The negative pole fires retrospectively on clauses describing the mental retrieval, recollection, or forgetting of past information (e.g., 'remember', 'recall', 'forgot'), as well as idiomatic expressions describing the passage or elapsing of time (e.g., 'went by', 'time flies', 'passed since'). It remains inactive on physical motion, non-recollective cognitive states (such as knowing or perceiving), and identical function words in non-temporal or non-memory contexts.

Fires when the text talks about the complement of a set that is already on the table - how much else there is besides the item just named. Strongest on exclusion/addition connectives aimed outside the mentioned item ('apart from / aside from / other than / besides / except for / beyond that/this/X,', peaking on the anaphor or on the comma that closes the phrase), on negative-polarity remainder quantifiers ('no other', 'nothing/little else', 'nothing/little more', 'no further', 'nothing besides'), and on exhaustiveness predicates ('that's / that is it/all', 'that's not all', 'X is all you need/said/have'); it stays inactive where the same words name no set - spatial 'apart/aside/beyond/next', positive 'other/else/more' ('other people', 'much else', 'more questions'), bare exclusives ('the rest', 'the last', 'sole', 'complete'), and other connectives ('because of that', 'before that', 'despite that', 'moreover', 'in addition').

This pole fires when the current token is a locally predictable continuation of the preceding 1-3 tokens, typically clause-glue function words (and/but/a/of/et) extending a well-formed phrase or a frozen collocation/completion (import->numpy, mg->of, pinch->of salt, ORDER BY->name, complete sentence->period); the same token in a surprising or ungrammatical left context fires substantially less.

Fires retrospectively on the first token of a locally licensed phrasal continuation — a prepositional argument or adjunct, auxiliary or copula complement, determiner-licensed noun, list-continuation quantifier, or clause-closing punctuation or tag — when the preceding 1-3 tokens license that continuation; the same token without such local licensing fires weakly or not at all.

The pole detects the stock 'more information / ask us / get in touch' formulae of written prose and peaks on their cue words: 'more'/'further' inside a purpose phrase ('For more information/details, ...' or '... for more details'), 'any' in 'if you have/need any ...', 'to' in 'do not hesitate to ...', and 'about'/'concerning'/'regarding'/'on' linking 'questions' to its topic. It does not fire on the bare directive itself ('Contact us', 'Visit our website', 'Click here'), on the same words in argument position ('she asked for more information', 'he did not hesitate to contact me'), or on ordinary conditionals ('if it rains'); because the peak is at the cue word, a fronted 'For more ...' is already active even when the continuation turns out not to be informational ('For more than twenty years').

Fires where a formatted document steps back out to a shallower structural level after content: the leading whitespace plus delimiter of a line that dedents relative to the line above it in code, markup or data (a dedented line fires ~2.0 whether it closes a tag or opens one, while the same line at the same indentation without the dedent fires ~0.5; strength grows with depth, nested JSON/HTML at depth 1->4 giving ~0.8->~4.4), and in prose documents the line-initial section index that resumes a numbering scheme after the previous section's body ('2.'/'II.' after a '1.'/'I.' section: 3.8 with the earlier index and a body, 0.9 without it). It is near zero in flat prose, at same-level or indent-increasing lines, and at confident but non-structural continuations.

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that supplies specifying material inside a short locally-licensed phrase: a preposition after its verb or noun head (sat on, boils at, calls for, converts into), an attributive modifier after a determiner, degree-word or quantifier frame (a young, the cold, of heavy, so fast), or a content word completing a fixed quantity, comparative or word-piece frame (than five, three times, at least, re-election, h+iked, 3+.). Most of its drive comes from the 1-3 preceding tokens, so the same surface word fires weakly or not at all when that licensing left context is removed or replaced.

This pole fires on degree/comparison phrasing that qualifies how strongly a property holds: a degree modifier with a gradable head ('too'/'a little'/'a bit' + adjective, adverb or quantifier - 'a little too neat', 'a few too many', 'too much for them', 'too deeply ingrained'; adjectival 'enough'; the 'the X-er the Y-er' correlative), with the peak on the modifier, on its head, or - highest - on the function word that opens the phrase's complement ('to'/'be' in 'too long to be sent', 'for' in 'too neat for my taste', 'to' in 'general enough to treat'). It also fires on 'if' conditionals (peak on the following subject/copula, as in 'if something is ...'), on hedged modals ('seems like it ought to ...') and on the newswire byline 'Name (@handle)' at its closing parenthesis, whereas plain factual predication and bare intensifiers ('The book is neat', 'The book is very neat') leave it near zero.

This pole fires at the final token of a highly constrained local formula — a frozen collocation or compound (triangle inequality, heavy rain, sea level, fell silent), a fixed function-word frame (According to, from X to Y, N times a day), or a boilerplate closer — where the peak token is strongly predictable from the preceding 1-5 tokens; the same token in an unconstrained context activates it weakly or not at all.

The pole fires on pieces of a compound token that the tokenizer splits, not on the words themselves: its peaks (0.3-1.0 of max) are the non-initial pieces of an unspaced dotted path, CamelCase or snake_case name - '.io' in 'java.io.File' (0.63), '.factory' in 'org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanFactory' (1.06), 'Utils' in 'SessionUtils' (0.43), '_SIZE' in 'MAX_SIZE' (0.47), '::' in 'Gem::Specification', '.support' in 'android.support.constraint' (0.54) - and the digit pieces of an ISBN-13-shaped number beginning '978' ('Order 9780008318543' 0.69, 'Order 9781402894626' 0.68), while the same morphemes written as separate words ('class Session Utils {' 0.05, 'max size' 0.10, 'com google gson Gson' 0.30) or other 13-digit numbers ('Order 8472910563123' 0.11) fall by 0.26-0.90 of max; a second, weaker route (0.2-0.6, straddling the active threshold) fires on clause-seam connectives in expository prose (' and' 0.24, ' or', ',', possessive '’s'). It is a graded dial rather than a detector - 65% of scanned tokens are below 0.031 and the 99th percentile (0.248) only just clears the 0.25x max threshold (0.233), so about 2% of ordinary text counts as active - and free-standing content words, code keywords ('public', 'static', 'int'), plain short sentences and document-initial tokens stay at or below ~0.15 of max; the extremes come from both SwiGLU sign regimes (g+u- for the identifier pieces, g-u+ for the connectives) and the promoted-token lens is incoherent (Jacobian kurtosis 3.2, logit/Jacobian overlap 0), so I claim the input feature only, not a specific next-token effect.

Fires on the word that expresses how often or at what rate an event happens, when it modifies an event that comes after it: indefinite-frequency adverbs placed before the verb ('Do your emotions sometimes/often/occasionally/frequently [rarely, usually, regularly weaker] dictate', strongest inside questions and weak in plain declaratives), the rate article or quantifier before a unit ('three times a year', 'twice a day', 'every 5 minutes', 'X percent of the time', 'spending more and more time'). It also fires on the closely related 'afraid/scared/reluctant to' (an inclination about whether the action will happen). It stays near zero for non-frequency adverbs (really, also, personally), for 'never' and 'always', for 'per'/'this' in place of the rate 'a', for sentence-initial 'Sometimes', and for frequency words after the verb ('go to the park often').

Fires on the token that completes a two-member, same-kind parallel: the second participant of the same animate kind in a coordinated, subordinate or comparative frame (doctor->nurse, chef->waiter, dog->cat, 'taller than his brother'), a second member carrying a repeated title or noun (Dr....Dr., Sen....Sen., CEO...CEO, northwest->southwest soldier, 44->39-year-old, 'and a man' after 'a 44-year-old man'), a place pair in an event or comparison frame (Berlin...visited Paris, 'more canals than Hamburg'), or an anaphoric re-invocation of an already-introduced item ('so is George', 'and if so', 'that of'), often peaking on the determiner, comma or title directly before that second mention. It stays near zero for complementary script-role pairs (doctor-patient, teacher-student, judge-witness, owner-dog, 'her plumber'), single entities, pronoun-only mentions and inanimate co-hyponym pairs (sushi/ramen, apples/oranges); unlike the positive pole, which fires on open-set remaining-member references ('other', 'others', 'two') and promotes 'EVERY'/'ALL', this negative pole's Jacobian lens promotes closed-pair vocabulary ('Both', ' respectively', 'the former/both-sides CJK') and suppresses universal quantifiers (' EVERY', ' ALL', ' ANY'), so it is retrospective second-of-pair detection whose output prepares aggregation vocabulary, and the three former hard negatives ('Berlin...Paris' 0.80, 'ordered another coffee' 0.37, 'the owner' 1.07) are covered and predicted active.

The negative pole fires retrospectively on the head of a dependent phrase that attaches to material already given on its left: most strongly the verb of a post-posed participial / shared-subject second predicate after a complete clause ('She sat by the window, watching the rain' 4.2; 'broke down crying' 1.7; 'both men pacing restlessly' 1.1), and likewise the complement of a light verb, command or API call ('take a look', 'check to see', 'curl -X GET', 'new SqlDataAdapter') or a property name continuing a declaration block already opened ('...top: 0; width: 100%' 1.6). The same word as the sentence's own main predicate, fronted before its host, or in a self-contained phrase stays near background ('Watching the rain, she sat by the window' 0.7 vs 4.2; a lone 'width: 100%' 0.04 vs 1.6), so the pole encodes right-branching attachment to already-built structure rather than the token itself.

Fires on the token that completes a locally predictable construction set by the preceding 1-2 tokens: a noun's fixed complement (triangle->inequality, pinch->of), a verb's expected particle or preposition (sat->on), a number's unit (500->mg, 12->percent), or a clause/list-linking comma. The same surface token (of, on, comma) stays low when the preceding context does not predict it.

Fires on a word naming a positive, desirable quality or successful outcome (good, easy, laudable, pleasing, trustworthy, survive, properly, option, better) when it is the evaluated predicate of a clause, and much more strongly when that predicate is negated, hedged or contrasted (isn't ... at all easy, hardly a pleasing, will never survive, laudable--but, wasn't an option). The negative-valence antonym in the same slot (hard, painful, collapse, bad, dangerous) is predicted inactive, as are neutral tokens.

Retrospective detector for the slot-filling token that completes a conventional 2-4-token functional frame set up in the preceding ~4 tokens (count plus preposition plus ordinal such as 'twice in the second', range endpoint such as 'from 9 a.m. to 5', dosage plus frequency such as 'amoxicillin three', requirement 'must contain at', or copula/quantifier/determiner plus content word such as 'contract was void' and 'pinch of salt'); the same surface token without those licensing words stays low.

Fires on a segment token (usually starting with '.', '/', '-' or a version digit) two or more segments into a URL, namespace URI or dotted/slashed import path when the segments before it spell a familiar, often-copied boilerplate string, so the segment completes a memorized canonical path: schemas.android[.com], msdn.microsoft.com/en[-us], code.jquery.com[/jquery], github.com/Azure[/go], android.support.v[7], django[.db], org.apache.commons.net[.]. Replacing an earlier segment with an unfamiliar name (example, zorblat, x9) mostly removes it, generic URLs and file paths (www.google.com/search, C:\Users\..., com.example.myapp) and ordinary prose stay near zero, and memorized prose or message boilerplate ('error: no known class method', traceback 'line 10,') gives only weak to moderate activity.

This pole fires most on a token that is the locally predictable completion of the immediately preceding 1-2 tokens (an idiomatic bigram or collocation such as fell silent, chemical energy, on the, or heavy rain); the identical token in an unpredictable local bigram context activates less. It is retrospective: the Jacobian lens shows no coherent promoted token set (kurtosis 3.4, 0% logit agreement), so it reacts to the just-completed phrase rather than preparing an upcoming token.

The negative pole fires while a fixed, formatted element of a document is being completed: on the run of '=' that underlines a one-word section title ('Introduction
====', 'Abstract
====', 'Methods
===='), on the first token of the line that follows a 'To:'/'cc:' email-header block (normally the next field name, 'Subject'), on a forum answer's opening word immediately after the 'A:' marker ('So', 'First', 'Correct'), on a legal caption's party-role word ('Plaintiff-Appellee'), and on 'Content-Type' inside a 'http-equiv="..."' meta tag; a schema's own field word also fires when the same sentence names the schema ('the email subject'). It stays near zero on those words in ordinary narrative prose, on ordinary sentence-initial words, on markdown '#' headings and bullets, on code keywords, tags and punctuation, on hard-wrapped line breaks, and on header blocks made only of 'From:'/'Date:' lines.

N917+ fires, retrospectively, on the token where text stops being written as an ordinary word and is instead spelled out piece by piece by a surface convention: the digit that opens a group inside a formatted numeral ('more than 20,|0|00 artifacts' 0.89, versus 0.23 for '20000' in the same sentence), the non-initial piece of a hyphenated or locant technical compound ('at' in 'HIV-|patients' 0.84 against 0.13 for 'HIV patients'; 'im' in '5,6-di|methylpyrazine' 0.33), or a piece of a long dotted/slashed or boilerplate string ('.lua' inside a 22-token fontloader package path 0.41; ' License' in 'Apache License, Version 2.0' 0.39 but 0.07 in 'License plates'). The peak is the first token of that spelled-out run, the rest of the run carries a decaying tail (0.89 -> 0.49 -> 0.00 across '20,000'), and the same surface token written as a plain word, plus ordinary prose, stays near the ~0.07 background.

Fires on the lexical word 'object' itself: whenever the current token is one of that word's surface tokens — 'Object', ' Object', 'object', ' object', 'objects', ' objects', 'Objects', ' Objects', '_object', '.Object', or the 'Object'/'object' that an identifier splits off (myObject, restore_object, Object.create, List<Object>, API_JSON.Root[Object], KtClassOrObject) — in code or prose and in either the noun or the verb sense, peaking at 0.7-1.0 of max for capitalised 'Object'/'Objects' and 0.4-0.65 of max for lowercase forms. Words that merely contain the letters but tokenise elsewhere ('objective', 'objection', 'objectively', 'objectId', 'JSONObject', 'django.objects') stay far below the line, as do specific object nouns (chair, table, car, rock, dog) at the 0.02 floor and lowercase generic thing-nouns (thing, entity, item, file, material, molecule, document) at 0.05-0.20 of max; only capitalised plurals of that generic set (' Files', 'Materials', 'Things', ' belongings', 0.26-0.38 of max) clear the 0.25 active line, and a bare no-space 'Object'/'objects' opening a text is the weakest firing form (~0.43 and ~0.19 of max).

A layer-0 lexical detector for the 'basically' neighbourhood: it peaks on the token ' basically' itself (5.8-6.0 against the 6.3 max) and fires on the words that qualify something as coarse, approximate, general or simplified - the 'bas-' root (basic, basics, basis, base(s), based, baseline, basal, basement, Basicamente) and qualifiers such as roughly/rough, essentially, mainly, general/generally, brief(ly), broad(ly), largely, mostly, fairly, pretty, simple/simply, plain, bare, crude, generic, vaguely, gist, summary, breakdown, overview. It stays at its 0.1-0.4 background floor when a different word carries the same meaning (foot of the mountain, cellar, foundation, essence, core, substance, effectively, precisely) or for precise/technical vocabulary (exactly, technically, arguably, usually, typically, coarse, imprecise, database, baseball), so label from the lexical item, not from the concept.

Fires retrospectively when the current token presents communicative encoding of mental or non-verbal content — verbs like describe, express, interpret, translate, represent or imagine, or nouns naming the medium or content (email, english, thoughts, mind, sense, picture, idea). The same syntax around a purely physical or manual action does not drive it.

This pole fires on the token that completes a strongly constrained, conventionalized backward-looking construction: a verb subcategorization (consists of, entitled to the), a fixed formula or boilerplate elaboration (newly discovered, This includes, treatments including), or a code compound/directive (using namespace, add_library, node_modules). Strength is graded by how well the wider passage supports that construction; the same token in an incongruous frame stays near zero, and content after the peak has no effect.

This pole fires when the current token resolves a conventionalized two-part nominal: the second half of a compound word (side-kick, black-smith, file-system, Viol-in, nucleophil-ic, dist-al, short-stops), the completion of a fixed modifier-noun collocation (power steering, private key, the other side, receiver end), or the hinge/second member of a binomial pair (President and Vice, mesial and distal, Harry and Ramona). Activation is driven by the constraining partner word in the immediately preceding context, so swapping that partner for a non-collocating word collapses activity while distant rewrites leave it intact.

L10/N286's negative pole fires on the token that carries temporal reference for its clause - the word that states when, for how long, how often, or in what order in time the statement holds: temporal nouns and span words (year, time, era, century, season, period, past, history), frequency/duration and deictic adverbs (always, often, sometimes, usually, never, ever, again, nowadays, today, earlier, later, before), and temporal adjectives/ordinals (early, later, old, medieval, first, second, last). It is not a detector of the scan's particular trigger tokens: any temporal-reference word fires it (annually, era and never were never seen in the scan), while non-temporal words that can fill the same slot (only, main, mainly, mostly, overall, story, centre) leave it near zero, and the response is graded by temporal span and past-orientation (past > next; year/era/century > month/week/morning). The pole reads the word already present at its own position (retrospective), and a passage that already carries temporal anchors about recurring or historical events raises the gain on a later time word.

Fires on low-information continuation tokens (copula is, pronouns I/you/he, determiners/relativizers the/that/as, or structural separators slash, comma, newline, ().) when the token merely continues or elaborates a referent or clause established in distant earlier context; stays low when the same surface token starts a new sentence/topic or carries new lexical content itself.

The pole fires on the concept of a public announcement or news item: information being announced, disclosed, posted or passed on to an audience, peaking on the words that name the item (announcement, notice, press release, statement, news, updates) and rising equally on the verb frames that do the same job when no such noun is present ('to inform', 'let you know', 'keep you posted', 'stay up to date', 'made public', 'share the news with everyone'). It stays low when the same content is framed as a directive or a non-disclosing act or medium (a warning or advisory, a speech, a memo, a report or raw data, academic 'published'), so it tracks disclosure-to-an-audience rather than the literal tokens.

This pole fires retrospectively on passages describing a formally attested collective procedure: a population being surveyed or sampled (surveyed N citizens, a survey conducted among randomly selected members), a choice being elected or voted on by members, or a protocol, decision, or message being approved or signed by a committee or key. Removing the attestation verb while keeping the numbers and group nouns collapses activity; edits outside such procedures do nothing.

The pole fires on the tokens by which a passage marks the participants or the outcome of a sports competition: a team's, club's or school's name or nickname ('North Carolina', 'Duke', 'Real Madrid', 'the Yankees', 'Boilermakers'), the fixed side designators 'home/away/visiting team' and 'home/away side', two team names coordinated as a subject ('Duke and Yale', 'Michigan State and Purdue'), a field of entries ('athletes from 23 countries', '23 National Olympic Committees'), and a game's score line ('89 – 72'). It is silent when the same place, institution, person or company names are not read as competitors ('I grew up in Michigan', 'He studied at Duke and Yale', 'Madrid and Barcelona are cities'), and on named individual athletes ('Nadal beat Federer'), generic 'team' ('the team bus', 'the basketball team') and sports words that name no participant or result ('the tournament was cancelled', 'the Olympic Games').

The pole fires on general, normative claims about the accountability and integrity of public institutions, the officials who run them, and the systems the public relies on: statements that power is abused or corrupted, that agencies, officials or elections are unaccountable, untrustworthy or open to interference, or that oversight, transparency and safeguards are needed against such abuse or human error. The same vocabulary inside a report of a specific incident (who resigned, was charged or jailed on which day) or in ordinary politics (campaigns, budgets, votes) leaves it near baseline.

Fires retrospectively on the token that grounds a just-mentioned generic place, building, institution, office or subunit category to a specific real-world referent: either the proper-name completion (e.g. 'Church' in 'Christ Church', 'Ville' in 'Hotel de Ville', 'Hospital' in 'University College Hospital') or the preposition linking the category to its specific name (e.g. 'of' in 'Department of Statistics', 'in' in 'neighbourhood in the city'). The same function words or nouns without a specific institutional or spatial referent (a pile of statistics, a memory in the city, a local church, a hotel lunch) activate it weakly or not at all.

This pole fires on the semantically decisive content word of a factual or definitional statement — the proper name, technical term, or number that delivers the sentence's key fact (e.g. Paris in 'the capital of France is Paris') — and stays near zero on function words, generic nouns like thing/stuff/here, and on the same content words placed in narrative or non-factual frames.

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes a stereotyped, conventionally fixed multi-word chunk: a news/publishing attribution frame ('Web posted', 'Story highlights', '[Name], [title], said', 'told [outlet]') or a code/legal boilerplate formula (CSS declaration, license header). It summarizes roughly 20 preceding tokens of formulaic context, so keeping the peak token but breaking the conventional frame collapses activation, while changing only the content after the frame does not.

Retrospective detector of a discourse pivot: the pole fires on a contrast/update marker (but, however, sentence-initial Now/Next, or a but/how/what/why question) only when the preceding context establishes a success, expectation, concession, or completed background item and the peak introduces its limitation, exception, unresolved remainder, or next development. The same surface tokens without that two-part setup (plain 'and'-coordination, intra-clause 'but', adverbial 'right now', or a question asked without prior concession) stay quiet.

This pole fires retrospectively when the just-read token completes a sequence-onset or first-item marker: an explicit ordinal (first/First/main), a series label numbered 1 (Experiment/Group/AIM/Part 1), an origin point (began in YEAR, onset years, to date), or a defining-core noun phrase; its output then promotes sequence-initial discourse tokens (First, firstly, 首先) and suppresses continuation tokens (again, further, another).

This negative pole fires on tokens inside a specialist technical name or code rather than on ordinary English: eponymous or measured terms ('Apgar score', 'Knudsen number', 'Hartmann number', 'serum CD62p'), code identifiers and file paths ('getElementById', 'load_backend', 'db/utils.py'), URL queries ('item?id='), citation keys ('Jungman1996') and patent or error numbers ('50-32785'), typically on the word-piece that carries the term's distinguishing content. It stays near zero on ordinary vocabulary, including the same head nouns used generically ('the number of the flow', 'the score was recorded') and on everyday narrative, and it is strongest inside technical or scientific documents.

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that carries a negated or opposite value: a minus-signed number (the '-' and especially the digits right after it, as in 'x is -3', 'from 5 to -5', 'from +5 to -5', or a minus-led second equation in a two-equation 'Solve A, B' system) and a word that reverses the one just used inside a parallel frame ('My Enemy, My Friend', 'encrypted ... decrypted', 'hired ... fired', 'positive ... and negative'). It stays at baseline for the corresponding positive value ('5 to +5', 'x is 3'), for a synonym or unrelated replacement in the same frame ('My Enemy, My Rival', 'My Enemy, My Cat') and for a plain repetition ('My Enemy, My Enemy'), and its output direction suppresses the counter/opposite/reverse vocabulary (counter, opposes, contradiction, 相反) rather than promoting a particular upcoming token.

This pole fires on tokens that sit inside source-code passages: type and method signatures (e.g. 'void'), member accesses ('.Fill', '.set', '.next', '.fetch'), object references ('$this', 'self'), template tags ('csrf_token'), and block-structure whitespace that closes code blocks, across programming languages. It reads accumulated preceding code context (most input attribution lies far before the peak), so the same tokens in ordinary English prose stay near zero.

Fires on prose in the proverb / maxim / slogan register: a clause that asserts a general truth about people, conduct or the world with a generic subject and no particular referent (proverbs, sententiae, advertising slogans, song-lyric maxims, famous aphorisms), and not on narrative, reportive, instructional or factual-descriptive prose about specific people, events or objects. The register is what matters, not fame or wording: invented maxims of the same shape fire as strongly as well-known ones, while the same content recast as a report of one incident falls to zero.

This pole detects search/listing result-count displays: text that reports how many items a search, listing or pagination produced — pagination and summary lines ('Showing 1 - 20 of 350 results', 'Search results: 1 - 10 of 55', 'Displaying 20 of 350 results', 'Results 1 - 1 of 1', 'Page 1 of 35') and result-count sentences ('Found 350 matching results', 'The search found 123 results', 'Showing 25 results per page'). It peaks on the numerals and the adjacent function/count words (' -', ' of', ' results', digits) inside such a frame, while numerals in ordinary narrative prose ('The experiment produced 123 results', 'There were 350 people at the event') and bare labeled numbers ('Order number 12345', 'Price: $1,234') stay inactive; page-view/session counters (e.g. 'has viewed by 51 users', 'based on 27 sessions') fire when a page-template context supports them but are weak and unreliable in isolation.

This pole fires retrospectively on the closing/boundary token (')', em/en dash, hyphen-dash, colon, or equivalent separator) that terminates a prefatory header such as a news dateline, byline/source tag like CITY (OUTLET), title label, or code/license preamble, marking the transition from header metadata into body text; it requires the location/outlet/label context before the boundary, not just the punctuation alone.

This pole fires on passages that specify an input: text that names data, a parameter, field, file format, record, application or item of evidence and states the form, type or requirement it must satisfy (e.g. 'the file format of X is not fasta: the first character is ...', 'Argument must be a string', 'Start and end are the two required parameters', 'the filing of a complete application', 'the operator supplies the input parameters'). Narrative, descriptive or conversational prose on the same subject - and prose about outputs, results or summaries instead of inputs - stays inactive.

N3782+ is a template/boilerplate detector rather than a word detector: it peaks on the slot token where a fixed, conventional construction commits to its continuation - the argument separator inside an SDK call idiom (`tracing.EndSpan(ctx, sc, err)`), the linker before a bug-tracker status label (`mark the bug as ___`), the copula of an administrative verdict (`For the reasons stated above, ... is ___`), the `multiple of` slot of a repeated MATH question - and it strengthens with each instance of that same formula in the preceding context. Strength is set by the formula, not the filler: swapping the filler leaves the peak untouched (UNCONFIRMED -> RESOLVED, denied -> granted -> purple all give the identical value) while breaking the formula removes 0.21-0.73 of max (fmt.Println for tracing.EndSpan, `as` -> `is`, `multiple of` -> `divisor of`, dropping the reason clause); it is retrospective, since zero-ablating the pole moves next-token logits by KL <= 0.006 and the promoted `return`/`result`/`setResult`/`Success` tokens never follow the peaks.

The negative pole fires when a clause quantifies a named measurable magnitude, i.e. a measure/quantity term (length, radius, diameter, distance, volume, weight, count, number, amount, price, cost, revenue, sales, duration, frequency) that is the subject or possessor in a statement giving or changing its value: it peaks on the copula or change verb carrying the value (' is' in 'the length of the pipe is 5 meters', 1.24; 'the count of students is 300', 1.53; ' rose' in 'the price of the box rose by 5 dollars', 0.51), on the measure word itself when the quantity is being named (' radius', 'angle', 'Einwohnerzahl'), and on a numeric field name in an assignment ('WHERE id=...', 0.98; 'index_(0)'); its opposite pole instead peaks on the operator/bound side of the same statements (' &', ' /', 'negative sign', 'upper limit', 1.9-2.2). It is the quantifying that fires, not the words: 'the color of the pipe is 5 meters' (0.10), 'the pipe is 5 meters long' (0.05), 'we measured the length of the pipe carefully' (0.22) and 'the box is bigger than the bag' (0.07) all stay below the 0.37 active line, and the pole's ablation shifts next-token probability by only ~1e-4 KL, so the claim is retrospective.

Retrospective detector for elaborative continuation within an ongoing exposition: it fires on the token that adds a non-first parallel or dependent expansion to already-introduced material, such as a second coordinated element after 'and'/'or', a serial or enumerating comma (including Chinese ，/ Japanese 、), or a resultative, attributive or predicative continuation (e.g. causing, organized, featured) extending the same entity or event. It stays low on sentence onsets, first list items, or the same lexical token presented without a parallel antecedent.

N7269+ fires where a piece of written text stops composing content and reproduces a ready-made, conventional formulation: the fixed status-of-knowledge formulae of research and institutional prose ('X is still debated/controversial', 'remains to be established', 'Little is known about X', 'much of the literature/evidence') and the fixed record formats with which such documents date and cite themselves (labeled dates 'Submitted: September 24, 2013', case citations '741 F.3d 1367', statistical notation 'P<0.01', headings 'Materials and Methods'), with the peak on the frame's linker (the hedge's copula, the plain space between month and day, the '<' or digit of a P-value); a span is predicted active if it contains one of these frames and inactive if the same content is spelled out in free-running prose or casual speech. The filler is interchangeable - swapping the topic after 'Little is known about' leaves the peak at 0.81 and 'Submitted: April 17, 2014' matches 'Submitted: September 24, 2013' (0.58 vs 0.63) - while paraphrasing the frame away costs a third to four fifths of the peak (P<0.01 1.13->0.24, 'is still debated' 1.21->0.51, 'Little is known about' 0.81->0.15) and chat, plain code and first-order narrative sit near zero (0.07, 0.20, mean activation on ' discuss' is -0.47); it is retrospective, since zero-ablating the pole moves next-token logits by KL 4e-6 and no token is consistently predicted after its peaks.

The pole fires where a sentence specifies the physical properties of a concrete object: an attributive size, dimension, material or colour word on the noun ('wider aisles and a larger produce department', 'high ceilings, wide windows', 'a 14-inch display', 'made of dark wood'), or an explicit measure ('thirty centimetres across', 'two metres long', 'a fine pitch of a metal wiring'), with the peak usually landing on the function word that follows the modified noun phrase. It does not fire when the same objects are merely mentioned bare ('the aisles and the produce department'), nor on narrative action, abstract political or economic argument, or a bare date or count.

L16/N7886- fires on a gradable quality adjective: the word that states how much of a scalar quality a referent has, whether evaluative ('difficult', 'tough', 'good', 'uncomfortable', 'scary'), perceptual ('heavy', 'hot', 'loud') or size/strength ('big', 'large', 'strong'), in attributive or predicate position, while classifying adjectives that name a category rather than a degree ('wooden', 'American', 'annual': <=0.01 of max in the same frame), deadjectival nouns ('difficulty': 0.05) and bare numerals ('The value is 3': 0.06) stay near zero, and strength additionally rises with preceding description of the referent ('This is one tough place' reads 0.28 of max alone but 0.60 after 'The prison is a maximum security facility. It holds Death Row inmates.'). An explicit degree adverb directly before the adjective cuts it by half to three quarters ('very difficult' 0.28 vs 'difficult' 0.62), and the one high-strength non-adjectival regime is a value assigned to a spatial CSS property ('top: 0' 0.18, 'left: 0' 0.21, but 'margin: 0' 0.04 and 'font-size: 0' 0.00), i.e. the same degree-on-a-dimension reading; the pole is retrospective (peaks land on the adjective itself, the next token decays) and its Jacobian lens promotes no coherent tokens (overlap 0%, kurtosis 5.2), so it is not preparing an upcoming token.

This pole fires on tokens that continue a structured institutional or technical exposition — naming a listed component (syllabus, cover page), a header field (Date:), a role, affiliation or membership link (mentor for, listed by, official website), or a citation or reference pointer — when the preceding passage already establishes an organized informational frame such as a course catalog, event notice, governance text, reference list, or generated documentation; the same words in casual, narrative, or chatty prose stay nearly silent.

This pole fires on or just after a subordinating or relational marker (after, due to, if, when, upon, as, arrival of, replaced) when the preceding passage frames someone filling, inheriting, joining, or being selected for a role, spot, or individualized outcome, typically because another party is absent, injured, dead, withdrawn, disqualified, or displaced. The same markers stay near zero in neutral temporal, celebratory, weather, or routine passages with no substitution-or-selection frame, and the peak is driven by the preceding frame rather than the words that follow it.

The negative pole fires where a text is enumerating or paralleling things: at the punctuation that ends one member of a series and lets the next begin — a comma, semicolon, colon or line break between members ('A, B, and C', a label followed by its description, 'one ... and the other ...', 'the first is ... and the second is ...', 'divided into five age groups: 1-4 years, 5-9 years, ...') — or at the period that closes one member's description in an announced set ('there are two types ...; the first are ...'). It is weak in ordinary narrative, argumentative and expository prose with no series in progress (clause commas, relative clauses, sentence-final periods) and in a bare list of one-word items that no sentence announces; its write direction nudges continuation and alternative markers ('also', 'or', 'and', 'etc', 'instead', 'rather') rather than any specific next token.

The pole fires on the count/numeral token that states how much a thing actually contains or has, when an earlier clause in the same sentence has just given that thing's apparent, claimed or expected amount ("the bag looks like a single portion but really contains two portions"; "the sign says one lane, but the road actually has two lanes."), the peak landing on the actual-amount count. Neither half alone fires it: a bare count ("the bag contains two portions"), a bare appearance claim ("the bag looks like a single portion") and a plain quantifier ("all of the students") all stay inactive, so the cue is the apparent-versus-actual amount contrast rather than the token or the noun.

The pole fires on prefabricated rather than composed wording: the terse credit/apparatus formats that name a document's source — a byline ('By <name>', or a name alone on its line above the agency/role, e.g. 'Maria Sanchez' over 'Bloomberg News'), a photo credit ('<name>/<agency>', 'via AP'), a citation's '<surname>, ed.', and the head of a 'References'/'External links'/'Category:' block — and, at similar strength, conventional clause templates in running prose, above all a relative clause whose subject is focused by 'only' with a modal predicate ('the kind of view that only a grandmother can cook up', 'the road that only buses can use') and a clause-final elliptical modal ('like a proper movie should'). It falls to the floor (under 10% of max) when the same information is composed as an ordinary sentence ('Maria Sanchez of Bloomberg News wrote about the warning', 'Jane Doe took the photos for Reuters', 'which T H Grengy edited', 'external files'), when the template's 'only' becomes 'any' or its modal is dropped, and in plain narrative prose; the negative pole instead fires on the specific named agent a claim is sourced to ('analysts', 'Reuters'), not on the generic role nouns a composed sentence uses ('the staff', 'the news agency').

Fires at the onset of a sentence, usually paragraph-initial, that frames, evaluates, or redirects the preceding multi-sentence passage — an anaphoric discourse pivot headed by a demonstrative (This/That), a definite abstract noun (The contrast/focus/difference), or an evaluative/additive marker (also/just/so, Case in point) that comments on prior text rather than continuing the narrative.

N2133+ fires on the language of making, supporting or contesting a claim: the epistemic vocabulary in which a text states what is known, argued, assumed, disputed or in doubt (evidence, hypothesis, premise, criteria, valid/invalid, claim, submit, confirm, conclude, dispute, cause, 'not true'), and, in scientific, medical and legal writing, on the specialist term such a claim is made about (autosomal, meningitidis, falciparum, indisputable, aneurysm), with the peak on that word or on the function word introducing it, usually at its first sub-word chunk. It stays at its GELU floor on narrative, dialogue, instructions, plain description, sports reporting and simple promotional copy that make no claim, even when those contain the same learned words used descriptively or evaluatively ('the plot is linear', 'the company's prognosis', 'dedicated counsel', 'she read the diagnosis'); a single learned word or one bare general sentence ('every case is different') is not enough, so the clause needs a run of claim or specialist-assertion language.

Retrospective detector for noun-phrase specification: the pole fires on the token that introduces (passive by, in/of/a, list comma) or completes (nationality, kinship/role, brand/code/regnal designation, or specifying adjective/participle) a modifier that narrows which person, group, product, strain, or institutional variant is meant. It stays quiet on the same function words and slots when the modifier is generic rather than specifying, and needs tens of tokens of discourse context for full strength.

The pole fires retrospectively on the token that exits or completes a full noun phrase: prototypically a present-tense copula, auxiliary or possessive verb (is/are/has) immediately following a lexical-noun subject, and more weakly on other post-nominal heads (past-tense was, modals like will, lexical verbs like set, purpose prepositions like for, or nominal completions like Rico and year). The same tokens evoke little activation with no preceding nominal, and pronoun subjects, indefinite or degraded noun phrases, and impoverished discourse context all fire more weakly than full lexical-noun phrases in rich context.

This negative pole fires when the text has just completed a backward-looking temporal anchor: an elapsed-duration phrase grounding an event in the past ('a decade / 4 years / long ago', 'dates back to October 1983', 'around 500 years' before some reference point). Its output direction promotes past-distance continuation tokens ('ago', 'years', 'decades', Chinese equivalents such as ten-years-ago forms) and suppresses forward-temporal connectives ('thereafter', 'afterward', 'succeeding'), so it acts as a detector-and-reinforcer of past-anchored time reference rather than reacting to any single trigger word.

Fires retrospectively on the connector token (a preposition such as on/by/to, a comma, or the outlet-name token itself) that credits the source or venue of reported information in a news-attribution frame: reported/obtained by X, confirmed/told/stated to X, on/from X-news/site, or an outlet subject of reported. It responds to the sourcing frame already read, not to any single trigger word.

The pole fires on the token that discharges a frame opened by earlier cue words: disjunctive 'or'/'if' resolving an explicitly paired alternative set (any/or/all, whether/or/not, with/or/without, either/or, little/if/any), and the verb or particle completing a directive or complement-taking routine (to/do, need-to/understand, Let-me/think, Why/advertise/to, go/out, referred/to/as). The same token outside its frame does not activate it, and it also fires on the constrained continuation of other conventionalized routines such as titles ('It/Comes') and procedural formulae ('content/deleted').

This pole fires retrospectively when the preceding discourse reports information or work obtained from others -- polls, surveys, questionnaires, studies, findings, contributed or submitted material -- integrating that receiving/reporting context over tens of tokens. Its output direction then promotes obtain/receive-framed continuations (获得, 得到, obtain) and suppresses provide/offer-framed ones.

Fires retrospectively on status modifiers that classify a person's employment or participation role (volunteer, amateur, civilian, partner, contractor, assistant), an organization's commercial/nonprofit form (private, commercial, charitable, independent), or a work's licensing/access terms (voluntary, non-exclusive, public-private, affordable) when used attributively before the role, group, or work noun. It does not fire on generic adjectives without this employment/ownership/licensing meaning.

The pole fires when a passage puts an abstract object or concept into words: the peak lands on the verb, adverb or qualifier that carries a statement, definition, description or expression ('stated', 'defined', 'described', 'expressed', 'characterised', 'formulated', 'formally', 'explicitly'), most strongly in a passive or definitional frame about an abstract subject ('this problem can be stated as follows', 'the syntax can be formally defined', 'the theorem can be described in one sentence'), and more weakly on technical attributive qualifiers inside abstract noun phrases ('initial', 'statistical', 'typical-set'). It stays near zero on narrative action, concrete everyday predications, instructions, code, and on non-verbal predicates of the same shape ('can be measured', 'can be represented', 'can be painted').

This pole fires retrospectively when the text read so far frames an adverse outcome, hazard, defect, or risk — bodily injury or illness, safety violations, product defects, violence or infringement, errors and faults, or content warnings — with activation building over the framing phrase and typically peaking on the token just before the word that names the harm. Concern-laden nouns such as liver or wrinkles drive it only inside a worry or medical-harm framing, not in neutral uses (liver and onions, wrinkles in fabric), and its output direction promotes bilingual risk and harm vocabulary (risk, worries, concerns,隐患,风险) while suppressing positive-achievement tokens.

The positive pole fires on text that reports a statistical result or an epidemiological quantity: it peaks inside hypothesis-test and effect-size notation ('P<0.001', 'p = 0.03', 'OR = 1.34; 95% CI 1.10-1.63', 'SE 0.08', '80% power', '± 8.1') and on the measures such results are stated in (incidence, prevalence, cohort, lesion, morbidity, mortality), taking its peak on the digit or punctuation that completes the notation (the '.' of '0.001', the ';' after 'OR = 1.34'); a clinical value recorded for a patient ('temperature 38.5 C', 'blood pressure 140/90') is a weaker trigger of the same kind. It is a statistics detector rather than a citation- or medical-topic-register detector: 'Smith et al., 2020', '[1],[2]', Table/Figure references, qualitative-methods prose, narrative clinical text, non-statistical numbers in everyday prose (recipes, prices, bridge spans, sports scores) and 'clinical practice' prose all stay inactive, with adjacent LaTeX citation markup ('[@ref1],[@ref2]', peak about 3.6, half the statistical peaks) the one non-statistical trigger found, while the 'clinical practice' clause drives the negative pole instead (strength 19.7 on ' clinical'), so one sentence can be strongly positive on its p-value and strongly negative on its 'clinical practice' clause.

The positive pole fires at the first subword piece of a word the model cannot retrieve as a single token - a long, rare, technical or foreign word (psych|opathology, carp|enter, proph|ylaxis, sy|geplejerske, rel|apse, utf|-8, and the same onsets in Danish, Dutch, French and Portuguese text) - and, more weakly, on the grammatical words of formulaic legal phrasing (by/under in 'unless required ___ applicable law', of, de, los). Familiar single-token words of the same meaning (psychology, schizophrenia, doctor, baker) do not fire it, and the negative pole fires on the mirror-image onsets: all-caps acronyms and un-English orthography (B|PO, P|VR, SP|OT, p|izzeria, katakana).

The pole fires on web-page boilerplate: the stock site text that frames online content — copyright/rights and privacy/disclaimer notices, subscription and social-media calls to action, bylines and last-update/version stamps, price and spec listing lines, URLs and file paths, and formulaic recipe or how-to phrasing — peaking on the salient tokens inside those stock strings (' digit', ' this', ' our', ' Email', ' Self', ' beta', ' coming', ' water', ' to', ' https', 'rending', the bare space before a numeral). It is near-silent on narrative or expository prose, on isolated UI labels, and on the same words, dates, numbers or product names inside ordinary sentences; paraphrasing a template into ordinary prose collapses the activation, and the opposite pole's strongest examples are expository article text.

The pole fires on a token whose last character is the vowel letter o - Latin o/O, Greek omicron and omega (ο/ό/ω), Cyrillic о/О, katakana syllables with the vowel o (オ/コ/ソ/ト/ロ/...), Arabic و - when that token is a piece of a word the model is spelling out across several tokens rather than a whole familiar word: mid-word o-final fragments of rare, technical or foreign vocabulary (Alopiidae, allozyme, cyclophosphamide, Ploče, Françoise), URL strings, and Greek text written character-by-character. It stays near zero for any o inside a common whole-word token (to, of, on, no, so, two, who, also, into, do, too, video), for a rare word that is merely mentioned rather than expected ('The word Alopiidae'), and for an o that closes a word (word-final Greek ο); its output suppresses o-initial word-continuation tokens, i.e. it cancels the o it has just read.

This pole fires retrospectively on tokens that sit inside a familiar multi-token chunk: an interior, non-final segment of a memorized person or place name, title phrase, dotted/underscored/camelCase code identifier, or word-internal suffix run, where the exact preceding token predicts the current token and the current token predicts a specific continuation. It stays near zero on chunk-final tokens and on same-category substitutions that break the memorized sequence, while edits to distant words leave the peak unchanged.

This pole is a lookahead predictor of an upcoming verb of abrupt physical transformation of a concrete object or substance — fracture/release verbs (break, crack, shatter, burst, explode, pop, split, blow, collapse), thermal-change verbs (melt, boil, soften, glow, ignite, flake) and damage/dissolve — and it peaks on the token immediately before that verb: a modal or imminence word such as ' to', ' will', ' may', ' could', ' can', ' had', ' nearly', ' and', ' which', or the subject noun itself ('the chamber' before 'dim'). It is near zero before ordinary verbs ('going to call' 0.26, 'wanted to leave' 0.04), for animate or abstract subjects ('the meeting is about to start' 0.06, 'the company is about to launch' 0.03) and for metaphorical uses of the same verb ('the day is about to break' 0.20, 'the fever will break' 0.03); at its peaks zero-ablating the pole specifically removes burst/sh(atter)/crack/explode/blow/pop/split/boil from the next-token distribution, and a few token-level triggers (' reaction is' 13.6, '.K' in Kotlin code, ' K' in Turkish, ' Haw' in 'Hawke') remain unexplained.

Retrospective detector for sustained neuroscience discourse (medial-temporal neuroanatomy such as perirhinal/hippocampal/parahippocampal/entorhinal, and clinical neurology such as rolandic epilepsy, meningioma case reports, DBS, neuroimaging): it fires on the generic token that follows the technical phrase (a conjunction, copula or preposition like and/was/with, adjacent punctuation, or a mid-word subword continuation), driven by the preceding term plus long-range clinical context and insensitive to the token after the peak; matched cardiology, legal, and everyday passages with the same structure do not activate it.

The negative pole fires on clause-boundary tokens (the comma after a transition marker such as Now, the period closing a header such as Theorem or Proof, a paragraph break, or an opening quote) that close a completed setup or observation clause at a discourse pivot into the next directive, proof step, contrast, or quotation, with activation collapsing on the word after the boundary. Its output direction suppresses the default let/let's/consider continuation, so it acts as a brake on the let-step at such pivots rather than predicting which word comes next.

The negative pole fires on a past-tense or past-participle predicate token (' called', ' sat', ' stood', ' named', ' seen', ' hit', ' hurt', ' loved', ' like') when the clause's subject is a sentient, individuated being (a person or an animal), and falls toward baseline when the same predicate token is predicated of an inanimate or abstract subject. Measured peaks: 'The girl was called by the owner' gives 9.0 on ' called' versus 0.6 for 'The table was called by the owner'; 'The cat sat on the mat' gives 6.6 on ' sat' versus 0.0 for 'The report sat on the mat'; abstract subjects ('report', 'theory', 'table') stay at 0.0-0.8 while concrete inanimates are lower than sentient subjects but graded ('The car was called' 4.0, 'The rock was called' 2.9), and activity predicates under a sentient subject stay at or under the activity line ('The girl walked' 0.4, 'The boy ran' 1.2).

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a conventionalized multiword formula characteristic of edited informational prose: comparative and quantifying collocations (more than, every N years), separator-formatted numbers (1,000), and fixed specifying formulas (English language, an abbreviated title such as Ms. or Oct. plus name/date). The same peak tokens outside such formulas (often, plain 1000, textbooks, after, bare names) activate it only weakly, so the conjunction of the formula's parts predicts activity better than any single trigger token.

Pole N53+ fires on 'clean', 'clear', 'blank' and 'empty' in the sense 'free of dirt, marks, noise or unwanted content', and on the thing whose state that is: it peaks on the adjective itself (about 8-11 of its 17.6 maximum, e.g. ' clean' in any mid-sentence context) and carries onto, often peaking on, the following noun in conventional clean/blank phrases and as the object of cleaning verbs (clean water 10.6, clean hands 11.4, blank page 11.9, blank slate 28, clean record 12.5, clean break 12.1, 'clear the table' 5.0), while that noun position stays near zero when the same adjective carries a decency or abstract-standard sense (clean jokes 0.1, clean energy 2.7). It does not fire on rarer synonyms of the same concept (spotless, pristine, immaculate), on the antonym 'dirty' at the adjective position (1.2), or on derived forms (cleaner 0.9, cleaning 1.2, cleanliness 3.7), so it is keyed to this small lexical set in its literal sense rather than to the abstract concept of cleanliness.

Retrospective detector for conventional background-grounding formulae in expository text: it fires on the token completing a standard administrative place/org/title unit (Hospital Association, County Commissioner, National Forest) or a canonical origin/custody/operation predication (was established/founded in YEAR, is run by X, facility-subject appointed a director) or a temporal-anchoring formula (soon after, N years ago, after receiving + nominalization), driven by the preceding multiword frame. It stays quiet when the same head noun or verb appears in a foreground episodic frame with no grounding formula: published-news leads, personal routines, exercise run, bare after/elected, people-subject appointments, whistle-blowing titles, generic landscape nouns.

Fires retrospectively on a non-initial subword piece that continues or completes a person or place proper name (given name, surname, town, county, or country) whose stem was read in the immediately preceding token(s); the same subword pieces inside ordinary common words do not drive it.
